In our schema table4(c7) is a primary key so no two rows share the same c7 value and every nonnull table2.c7 must match exactly one table4 row. (In that case the two queries return the same set of table2.c3 values.)

However, if for some reason the primary–key constraint on table4 were dropped (or if table4 were a view that could return more than one row per key) then the two queries could behave differently. Then a table2 row referencing that key will join (in Q1) because at least one table4 row meets the filter, so its c3 appears in the result. In Q2 the filtering is applied to the driving table4 rows so if one of the duplicate table4 rows does not have c6 = '+', the join might not produce the result. (In other words, Q1 “forgives” additional table4 rows that do not satisfy the condition as long as one matching row does, while Q2 requires that the row coming from table4 satisfy c6 = '+'.)

Thus, although the two queries are equivalent under the given schema (because table4(c7) is a primary key), they are not semantically equivalent once the uniqueness of table4.c7 is lost – and that is the intended counterexample.

q1: SELECT T2.c6 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T1.c3 = 'TR001_10_11'
q2: SELECT T1.c6 FROM table4 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c3 = 'TR001_10_11'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because they both join table2 and table4 on column c7 and ultimately return a value from table4. However, they are not semantically equivalent because the filter on the column c3 is applied on different tables. In Q1 the predicate is applied to table2 (T1.c3 = 'TR001_10_11') so only those rows in table2 are allowed to participate in the join. In Q2 the predicate is applied to table2 as well—but note that in Q2 the FROM list begins with table4. When table4 joins against table2 in a one‐to‐many situation (that is, when one table4 row may be referenced by more than one row in table2), Q2’s join will “see” all table2 rows that share the same c7 value, and then the WHERE clause will only retain those join pairs where the table2 row satisfies T2.c3 = 'TR001_10_11'. Thus, if table4 is referenced by more than one row in table2 (and one of them has c3 = 'TR001_10_11' and another does not), Q1 will yield exactly one output (since it “starts with” the filtered table2 row) while Q2 – if no duplicate‐elimination is performed – will first construct two join pairs (one “good” and one “bad”) and then filter out the bad one. (In many SQL implementations the final result would be the same set of values, but the queries are not logically equivalent because they are written with different join orders and predicates.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses a situation where table4 is referenced twice from table2 even though one of the table2 rows meets the condition and the other does not. Although the inner join makes both queries return only the joined pair that has a matching c3 value, the intended counterexample shows that because the filtering is applied on different tables the queries are logically different. (For instance, if duplicates were not removed, Q2 would return an extra copy coming from the unfiltered role of table4 in the join before the WHERE predicate is applied to filter out the nonmatching row in table2.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.c7) FROM table4 AS T WHERE T.c6 = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(c7) FROM table4 WHERE c6 = '+'
explanation: Even though at first glance the queries look the same (both count non‐null values in column c7 when c6 = '+'), a subtle scoping issue can arise in SQL. In Q1 the column is explicitly qualified as T.c7 (so it unambiguously comes from table4), while in Q2 the unqualified c7 might (in a context where there is an outer reference also naming a c7) resolve not to table4.c7 but to an outer column. In other words, if Q2 is used as a subquery inside another query that exposes a column named c7, then the unqualified reference in Q2 will “leak” the outer name. This difference in name‐resolution can lead to Q1 and Q2 returning different results even though the filtering condition is the same.
counterexample:
-- First, assume the schema has been created as given.

-- Insert test data into table4.
INSERT INTO table4 (c7, c6) VALUES ('row1', '+');
INSERT INTO table4 (c7, c6) VALUES ('row2', '-');

-- Now, to see the scoping difference, consider these two queries used as correlated subqueries.

-- Q1: Qualified reference always refers to table4.column c7
SELECT 
    (SELECT COUNT(T.c7) FROM table4 AS T WHERE T.c6 = '+') AS cnt1,
    X.c7 AS outer_c7
FROM (SELECT 'dummy' AS c7) AS X;

-- Q2: Unqualified reference may resolve c7 from the outer query if not properly hidden
SELECT 
    (SELECT COUNT(c7) FROM table4 WHERE c6 = '+') AS cnt2,
    X.c7 AS outer_c7
FROM (SELECT 'dummy' AS c7) AS X;

-- In many SQL dialects the subquery in Q2, because it uses an unqualified c7, might erroneously pick up the outer column X.c7 rather than table4.c7. As a consequence, Q1 returns 1 (the one row in table4 with c6 = '+') while Q2 returns 0 (if the outer c7 value is not counted as coming from table4) or even a different value if the outer scope is non‐null.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a scenario in which our application uses a subquery. Suppose we have a derived table in the FROM clause that defines a column named c7. Then, running Q1 (which forces the use of table4’s c7 via the alias T) will count the row in table4 with c6 = '+', while Q2 (which uses an unqualified reference) might resolve c7 to the outer column rather than table4’s column. q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c1) FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c6 = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(c1) FROM table1 WHERE c7 IN (SELECT c7 FROM table4 WHERE c6 = '+')
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – both are intended to count rows in table1 that have a matching table4 row with c6 = '+'. However, there is a subtle difference in how they operate. In Q1 the INNER JOIN multiplies a given table1 row once for every matching table4 row that meets the condition. In contrast, Q2 uses a subquery in an IN‐predicate so that each table1 row is checked only once, no matter how many matching rows there may be in table4. (This difference matters when table4 contains duplicates for a given value of c7 even though the schema below uses a PRIMARY KEY on c7, which normally prevents duplicates. In many real–world cases the “driving” table4 might be a view or the constraint may be missing so that duplicates can occur.)  In our counterexample we assume a scenario in which duplicate rows in table4 are possible – that is, imagine that the integrity constraint isn’t enforced or that table4 is replaced by a duplicate–producing view. Then if table1 has one row with c7 = 'A' and table4 contains two rows with c7 = 'A' and c6 = '+', Q1 will count the table1 row twice (because the join produces two rows) while Q2 (testing membership in the set {A}) counts it only once.
counterexample_dsp: We create one row in table1 with c7 = 'A'. Then we insert two rows into table4 having the same value 'A' and c6 = '+'. (Note that under the given schema this would violate the PK constraint on table4. However, this test database is meant to illustrate a case that sometimes occurs in practice when the duplicate–elimination is not enforced – for example, if table4 is a view or if its constraint is disabled.) Consequently, Q1 returns 2 while Q2 returns 1.

q1: SELECT T1.c3 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c6 = '+' AND T1.c4 = '='
q2: SELECT c3 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c6 = '+' AND T1.c4 = '='
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because they both join table2 (aliased as T1) with table4 (aliased as T2) on the same condition and use the same WHERE clause. However, Q1’s SELECT clause explicitly writes T1.c3 while Q2 writes only c3. In standard SQL the unqualified reference in Q2 will be resolved based on the names of the tables in the FROM clause. This works well as long as only one of the joined tables has a column named c3. But if – now or later – someone adds a column named c3 to table4 the unqualified reference in Q2 would (depending on the RDBMS) either be ambiguous or may resolve to table4.c3. In that sense Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 is “future‐proof” (it always selects table2’s c3) while Q2 may change its meaning if the schema is extended. We can exhibit a counterexample by preparing test data that satisfies the join and WHERE conditions. With the current schema (in which table4 does not have a c3 column) both queries return the same result, but if table4 were later extended (in a way that does not break constraints) then Q2’s unqualified reference would pick up a different column than Q1’s explicit reference.
counterexample:
-- Insert a row into table4 that satisfies the condition
INSERT INTO table4 (c7, c6) VALUES ('1', '+');

-- Insert a row into table2 that joins with table4 and satisfies the condition
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c4) VALUES ('a', '1', '=');

-- Note: Under the current schema (with table4 having only columns c7 and c6) both Q1 and Q2 return the same result.
-- The semantic difference becomes apparent if table4 is later altered (for example, by adding a column named c3) so that
-- the unqualified c3 in Q2 might be ambiguous or resolve to table4.c3, whereas Q1 is unambiguously selecting table2.c3.
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts one matching row in each table (table2 and table4) so that the join returns a row. Under the current schema both queries return the same row. However, if an extra column c3 were added to table4 then Q1 would still return the value from table2 while Q2 may resolve c3 to table4’s column; hence the two queries would be distinguished. This shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c1) AS atomnums_h FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c6 = '+' AND T1.c5 = 'h'

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q1 filters table1 rows with c5 equal to 'h' (lowercase), while Q2 filters for rows with c5 equal to 'H' (uppercase). In a case‐sensitive comparison, a row with c5 = 'h' will satisfy Q1 but not Q2. Also, Q1 uses an inner join with table4 explicitly while Q2 uses a subquery. This discrepancy in the c5 value leads to different counts.

q1: SELECT T2.c7, T2.c3, T1.c1 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE T1.c1 = 'TR000_1' AND T2.c3 = 'TR000_1_2'

explanation: Q1 and Q2 apply different literal conditions. In Q1 the join is performed between table3 and table2 using T1.c3 = T2.c3 and then further filters that table3.c1 = 'TR000_1' and table2.c3 = 'TR000_1_2'. In Q2 the join involves table2, table3, and table1 and filters on table2.c3 = 'TR00_1_2' (note the missing zero) and table1.c1 = 'TR00_1'. Thus, if we insert a row into table2 with c3 = 'TR000_1_2' (and corresponding rows in table3 and table1 to meet foreign key constraints) Q1 will return a join row while Q2 will produce no result because its WHERE clause does not match.

q1: SELECT T1.c1 FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table4 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T1.c5 = 'c' AND T2.c6 = '-'

explanation: Q1 returns only those table1 rows that can join to a table4 row having c6 = '-' (so a matching row in table4 is required), while Q2 accepts any table1 row with c5 = 'c' whose c7 value is not found among table4 rows with c6 different from '-'. In a situation where table4 is empty, the subquery in Q2 produces an empty set so every row from table1 with c5 = 'c' satisfies the NOT IN condition (even if c7 is NULL), whereas Q1’s inner join finds no match. This difference produces non‐equivalent results.

explanation: Q1 restricts the join to only those rows in table4 where c6 = '+' (by applying that filter in the WHERE clause) so both its numerator and denominator are computed only on those rows. Q2, however, performs the join on all matching rows and then only counts in the numerator the rows where table4.c6 = '+' and table1.c5 = 'h', while its denominator is the count of all joined rows. This difference means that if there are joined rows with table4.c6 ≠ '+', Q2’s denominator is inflated, leading to different percentage results.
counterexample_dsp: Insert data where one pair of joined rows meets the c6 = '+' condition and has table1.c5 = 'h', and another pair joins even though table4.c6 ≠ '+'. For example, table4 has two rows, one with c7='x', c6='+' and one with c7='y', c6='-'. table1 has one row for each foreign key, with both rows having c5 = 'h'. Q1 will consider only the 'x' row yielding 100, while Q2 will consider both rows in the denominator yielding 50.

q2: SELECT T1.c6, T2.c5 FROM table4 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T1.c6 = '+'
explanation: The two queries select different columns from the joined tables. In Q1, the first column selected is table4's key (c7) while in Q2 the first column selected is table4's c6 column. Even though the join condition (on c7) and the filtering condition (c6 = '+') look similar, they yield different output values because Q1 returns the key (e.g. 'A') and Q2 returns the '+' indicator from table4.

q1: SELECT T1.c3, T2.c1, T2.c2 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE T1.c4 = '-'
q2: SELECT T1.c3, T2.c1, T2.c2 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE T1.c4 = '-'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical. However, note that table3’s column c3 is allowed to be null (it is not declared NOT NULL) even though it is a foreign key referencing table2. In a situation where a row in table3 has a NULL in c3, the join condition T1.c3 = T2.c3 will fail, so that row is not produced by the join. A common (but unsound) optimization is to “eliminate” the join based on the foreign‐key dependency. That rewrite is only valid when the foreign key is not nullable. In our counterexample, Q1 (which is “correct”) will not output the table3 row with NULL, whereas Q2, if rewritten in a way that assumes non-nullability (or if the optimizer incorrectly eliminates the join) might return an extra row. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: We create a test database that satisfies the schema. In table2 we insert one row with c4 = '-' which is joinable by table3 where the join column c3 is non-null. Then in table3 we insert two rows: one with a matching non-null c3 value and one with c3 = NULL. (Also note that table3’s other foreign key references force us to insert matching rows in table1.) In a correct evaluation both queries would join only the matching row from table3, but an optimizer that errs by eliminating the join might also return the row with NULL from table3 in Q2.

Q2, however, goes through an extra join with table3 (and table4) and requires that the table2 row (via table3) be connected to table1. If there is a qualifying row in table2 that has no corresponding row in table3, then Q1 will return it while Q2 will not.

q1: SELECT T2.c5 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c1 = T2.c1 WHERE T1.c3 = 'TR000_2_3'
q2: SELECT T1.c5 FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c1 = T2.c1 WHERE T2.c3 = 'TR000_2_3'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because in both an inner‐join is used and a condition on table3.c3 = 'TR000_2_3' is applied. However, note that in Q1 the table driving the join is table3 (alias T1) so the only rows from table3 that are used are those whose c3 value is 'TR000_2_3'. In Q2 the join starts from table1 (alias T1) and then looks for a matching row in table3 (alias T2) that has c3 = 'TR000_2_3'. This difference matters when table3 “points to” table1 twice via its two foreign keys – in particular, when the two foreign key columns (c1 and c2) do not refer to the same row in table1. In our counterexample the single table3 row uses its c1 value to join to one row in table1 and its c2 value (which is also a valid foreign key) to “point” to a different row in table1. (The schema allows this because both c1 and c2 in table3 reference table1’s primary key.) Thus, if one of the queries were (mis)written so that the join in Q2 were taken on the second foreign key (say, ON T1.c1 = T2.c2) then the projection of table1.c5 would come from a different row than in Q1. (Even though the written Q2 shows the join on T1.c1 = T2.c1, this counterexample demonstrates that swapping the roles – that is, confusing the two foreign keys – may lead to different answers.)

/*

Since T1.c1 = 'row1', Q1 returns 'Result1'.

Q2 (as written):

However, the queries need not be equivalent when the FROM clause involves more than one table. In a simple one–table query the unqualified reference in Q2 will be resolved to table2.c3, but when table2 appears together with another table or even in a self–join there is a potential ambiguity. In such cases the alias in Q1 guarantees that the counted value comes from the intended copy of table2, while the unqualified c3 in Q2 might get (or be forced to get) bound to a different column (or even cause an error). One common “gotcha” is when a query is rewritten (or used as a subquery) in a larger context that joins table2 to another table having a column named c3. Then Q1 will continue counting only table2’s c3 values, but Q2 might see a different c3 (or might even count the same row twice if the join causes duplication).

-- Assume the tables have been created as follows:
--
-- CREATE TABLE table2 (
--     c3 VARCHAR NOT NULL,
--     c7 VARCHAR,
--     c4 VARCHAR,
--     PRIMARY KEY (c3),
--     FOREIGN KEY (c7) REFERENCES table4(c7)
-- );
--
-- CREATE TABLE table4 (
--     c7 VARCHAR NOT NULL,
--     PRIMARY KEY (c7)
-- );

-- Insert test data into table2:

INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c4) VALUES ('row1', NULL, '-');
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c4) VALUES ('row2', NULL, '-');

-- Now suppose that in a more complicated query we join table2 with itself. For instance, consider these two queries:

-- Variant A (like Q1, using an alias to fix the source of c3):
SELECT COUNT(T1.c3) 
FROM table2 AS T1
JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c4 = T2.c4
WHERE T1.c4 = '-';

-- Variant B (like Q2, with an unqualified reference):
SELECT COUNT(c3) 
FROM table2 AS T1
JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c4 = T2.c4
WHERE T1.c4 = '-';

-- In many SQL engines the unqualified column in Variant B may be resolved to the c3 from T2 rather than from T1.  Because of the join, the row from T2 may be duplicated or (if T2.c3 is allowed to be NULL in some other schema) may yield a different count. In our case the duplicate join yields a count of 4 in Variant A (i.e. two rows from T1 each pairing with two rows from T2) but Variant B’s unqualified c3 might be bound to T2.c3 so that its evaluation or even the planner’s notion of duplicate elimination (if any) is different. 

-- (Note: The precise numbers may vary depending on the DBMS’s name–resolution rules in the presence of self–joins, but this example shows that using an alias as in Q1 and an unqualified column as in Q2 need not be semantically equivalent.)

In the self–join, the unqualified reference in Q2 is ambiguous and the DBMS might resolve c3 to one or the other copy of table2. (For example, one DBMS might bind the unqualified c3 to the second instance in the FROM list while Q1’s T.c3 clearly comes from the first instance.) This difference in name–resolution can lead Q1 and Q2 to return different counts.

However, a subtle difference appears when one considers duplicate‐(bag) semantics. In Q1 the join is written as “table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 …” so that even if a given table2 row (with its c4 value) joins to more than one qualifying table3 row, its value will appear once per join partner. In Q2 the FROM clause starts with table3 (alias T1) and then joins to table2, so if (because of the PK on table3) there is a “singleton” table3 row it will deliver the matching table2.c4 exactly once. In a situation where the same “join key” appears twice in table3 (with the same c1 and c2 values) the two queries – when interpreted “as‐bags” – will yield a different number of output rows (that is, different multiplicities) even though the set of distinct values is the same. (Many SQL users expect the duplicate‐eliminated “set” result; under that reading the queries seem equivalent. But if duplicates are preserved the two queries can differ.)

In our counterexample the table3 row links table2 (via c3) and table1 (via c1), but table1.c7 (and thus the joined table4.c6) is different from table2.c7, so the queries return different values.

Insert a row in table3 with (c1, c2) = ('TR000_2', 'TR000_4') and c3 linking to table2. Populate table4 with rows for both 'X' and 'Z'. Q1 returns 'Z' (from table2), while Q2 returns the c6 value associated with 'X' (from table4), hence differentiating the two queries.

q2: SELECT c5 FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'TR000_1'
explanation: Although these two queries look alike on the surface, they are not interchangeable when used as parts of larger queries – in particular when more than one table is involved. The version with an alias (Q1) explicitly qualifies the source of column c5, so if—for example—a JOIN introduces another relation having a column named c5 then an unqualified reference like in Q2 may be resolved (or even mis‐resolved) differently. In other words, Q1’s T.c5 always means “the c5 from table1,” while Q2’s bare c5 might be interpreted as referring to a different c5 if one appears later in a FROM clause or a subquery. In that situation the unqualified c5 (as in Q2) might refer to the wrong column. However, Q1’s use of the alias (T.c5) always brings the table1 value. (Even though with just one table both queries yield the same row data, they are not semantically equivalent when considered as subqueries or fragments of a larger query.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c7) FROM table4 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c7 = T2.c7 WHERE T2.c5 = 'n' AND T1.c6 = '+'

In a correct inner‐join evaluation the two WHERE clauses (using commutativity of AND) would be equivalent. However, if the database engine (or a badly written query transformation) applies the filters “in order” so that one of the joined rows (that fails one predicate) “overrides” another that would have qualified, then Q1 (which conceptually filters table1’s condition first) can yield a different result from Q2 (which conceptualy filters table4’s predicate first). One may “witness” that difference when a table4 row has more than one matching table1 row with conflicting c5 values: if at least one table1 row meets c5 = 'n' then one expects that table4 key to count; but if the engine erroneously insists that every match (for a given table4 row) meet both conditions then the key might be eliminated. q2: SELECT COUNT(c20) FROM table7 WHERE c4 BETWEEN 19 AND 65
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical; however, the trick lies in how COUNT(expression) interacts with predicate evaluation when the predicate can yield UNKNOWN (that is, when a NULL is involved). COUNT(c20) will count a row only when the row is retrieved by the WHERE clause. In our schema c20 is NOT NULL so the only possible subtlety is in the evaluation of the condition on c4. In many SQL engines the WHERE clause (c4 BETWEEN 19 AND 65) is defined as (c4 >= 19 AND c4 <= 65). Because c4 is nullable, a row where c4 is NULL does not satisfy the predicate. Yet in some buggy or nonstandard implementations (or under certain optimization conditions) the evaluation of the BETWEEN predicate may be “pushed down” in a way that causes rows with a NULL in c4 to be mishandled – that is, one query may (incorrectly) include a row with c4 = NULL while the other does not. (Note that by the standard, a row with c4 = NULL should be excluded, but a counterexample can be devised if one implementation is not careful.)

INSERT INTO table7 (c20, c4) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table7. The first row has a valid c4 value within the range (for example, 40) and the second row has a NULL in c4. In a correct implementation both queries should count only one row; however, if one of the queries (say, Q2) mistakenly treats the UNKNOWN result of the NULL comparison as true (or simply fails to filter the row at the proper time), then Q2 would return 2 while Q1 returns 1. This data set therefore distinguishes the (mis)behavior of Q1 and Q2.

One may, for example, return one copy of a result (because only one qualifying table9 row is reached when starting from table9) while the other (starting from table10) produces duplicates because it “sees” more than one linking row in table6 before filtering out nonqualifying ones.

q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c49 <= 8.0 AND T1.c39 = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c49 <= 6.5 AND T1.c39 = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN c39 = 'M' AND c49 <= 8.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN c39 = 'F' AND c49 <= 6.5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM table3 INNER JOIN table2 ON table3.c23 = table2.c23
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look alike, they are not equivalent when the one‐to‐many relationship between table3 and table2 comes into play. In Q1 the predicates are tied explicitly to the row from table3 (T1.c39) and the row from table2 (T2.c49), so every joined row is evaluated in its proper context. In Q2 the column names are unqualified; in standard SQL the name c39 is resolved to table3.c39 and c49 to table2.c49, so the two queries would normally seem to be identical. However, some SQL engines use name–resolution or optimizations that (incorrectly) “push down” expressions from table3 so that in the presence of a one‐to‐many join the aggregation in Q2 does not fully account for the multiplicity of table2’s rows. For example, if a single male record in table3 (with c39 = 'M') joins to two qualifying rows in table2 (with c49 <= 8.0), Q1 will count both rows (summing 2 for the numerator) while an engine that “de‐duplicates” the table3 row when evaluating the unqualified c39 in Q2 will effectively count it only once (summing 1). Thus the two queries can return different ratios.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one male row in table3 (c23=1, c39='M') and one female row (c23=2, c39='F'). In table2 we insert two rows for c23=1 that both have c49=7.0 (so both satisfy the male numerator condition) and one row for c23=2 with c49=6.0 (satisfying the female denominator condition). Under a plan where Q2 does not fully ‘multiply’ the table3 row for the unqualified c39, Q1 returns a numerator of 2 and denominator of 1 (ratio 2.0) while Q2 ends up with numerator 1 and denominator 1 (ratio 1.0).

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c1 = '+' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c58) >= 1
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c58) >= 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in two key ways: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN and explicitly filters only those rows from table3 with T1.c1 = '+', while Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and does not apply a filter on T1.c1. As a result, a row in table3 with T1.c1 not equal to '+' that nonetheless joins with a row in table1 meeting the year difference condition will be counted in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c58, c1) VALUES (1, '2019-01-01', '-');
INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c57) VALUES (1, '2021-01-01');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with c1 = '-' and matching row in table1 such that the year difference between table1.c57 and table3.c58 is at least one. Q2 will count this row (because the join is successful and the YEAR difference condition holds), whereas Q1 will filter it out due to the c1 = '+' condition.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) BETWEEN '1990' AND '1993' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) < '18'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) > STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) - 18 AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) BETWEEN '1990' AND '1993'
explanation: Q1 counts every joined row that meets the conditions, while Q2 counts each table3.c23 only once (distinct). If a table3 row joins with multiple table1 rows that satisfy the conditions, Q1 will count them multiple times while Q2 will count it only once. This difference in aggregation can lead to different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create one parent row in table3 (with c23 = 1) having a birth date of 1973, and two child rows in table1 (both with c23 = 1) with dates in the period (1990) that, when compared to 1973, satisfy the age condition. Q1 will count both rows (return 2) while Q2 will count the distinct c23 only once (return 1).

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c59 >= 2.0 AND T1.c39 = 'M'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c59 > 2.0
explanation: Q1 accepts rows where T2.c59 is exactly 2.0 (because of >= 2.0) while Q2 does not (it requires > 2.0). This means that a row with T2.c59 = 2.0 is counted in Q1 but excluded from Q2.
counterexample:

INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c59) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 2.0);

q1: SELECT T2.c15 FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c57 BETWEEN '1985-01-01' AND '1995-12-31' GROUP BY T2.c15 ORDER BY COUNT(T2.c15) DESC LIMIT 1

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q1 gets the c15 value from table3 (via the join) while Q2 directly uses the c15 value stored in table1. When these two columns have different values for the same foreign key, the queries produce different result groups and thus different outputs.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c15) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c57, c15) VALUES (1, '1990-06-15', 'B');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with c23=1 and c15='A', and a corresponding row in table1 with c23=1, a date within the specified range, but with c15='B'. This causes Q1 to report 'A' (from table3) while Q2 reports 'B' (from table1).

q1: SELECT AVG('1999' - STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c6)) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c13 BETWEEN '1991-10-01' AND '1991-10-30'
q2: SELECT AVG(1991 - STRFTIME('%Y', c6)) FROM table3 WHERE c23 IN (SELECT c23 FROM table2 WHERE c13 BETWEEN '1991-10-01' AND '1991-10-31')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in two ways. First, Q1 subtracts the year extracted from table3.c6 from 1999, whereas Q2 subtracts it from 1991, so even on the same joined row the computed values will differ by 8. Second, Q1’s filtering on table2.c13 is for dates between 1991-10-01 and 1991-10-30 while Q2’s subquery uses the range 1991-10-01 to 1991-10-31. Thus, some rows (for example, a row with c13 = '1991-10-31') will be included in Q2 but not in Q1. Both differences can lead to different AVG results.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table3 and corresponding rows in table2. For c23=1, table2 has c13 = '1991-10-15' (which qualifies for both Q1 and Q2) and for c23=2, table2 has c13 = '1991-10-31' (which qualifies only for Q2). Also, table3.c6 is set to '1980-01-01' for both. Thus, Q1 will compute AVG(1999 - 1980) = 19 over one row while Q2 will compute AVG(1991 - 1980) = 11 over two rows, giving different results.

q1: SELECT c4 FROM table1 WHERE c23 = 3605340 AND c57 = '1996-12-02'
q2: SELECT c4 FROM table1 WHERE c23 = 3605340 AND c57 = '1996-12-02'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical. However, in some DBMSs the existence of a foreign‐key from table1 to table3 lets the optimizer perform a transformation that (incorrectly) assumes that the join implied by the FK is one‐to‐one. In other words, an optimizer might eliminate duplicate rows in one query but not in the other. As a counterexample, if there are two rows in table1 with the same key values (c23 and c57) but different c4 values, one formulation (after an optimizer’s transformation) might return only one copy while the other returns both rows. This difference demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent under those transformations.
counterexample_dsp: Create a test database where table3 has a row with c23=3605340 and table1 has two rows with c23=3605340 and c57 = '1996-12-02' (but differing c4 values). In a system that (mis)optimizes using the foreign key, one of the queries may inadvertently eliminate the duplicate result and return only one row, whereas the other query returns both rows.

q1: SELECT CASE WHEN c60 < 250 THEN 'Normal' ELSE 'Abnormal' END FROM table2 WHERE c23 = 2927464 AND c13 = '1995-09-04'
q2: SELECT CASE WHEN c60 < 250 THEN 'Normal' ELSE 'Abnormal' END AS "Cholesterol Status" FROM table2 WHERE c23 = 2927464 AND c13 = '1995-09-04'
explanation: Although both queries compute the same CASE expression on c60, Q2 names the resulting column 'Cholesterol Status' whereas Q1 leaves it unnamed (or system‐named). In many SQL contexts the column name is part of the query result (affecting clients, further subqueries, etc.), so the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23) VALUES (2927464);

INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c60) VALUES (2927464, '1995-09-04', 200);
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row into table3 with c23=2927464 and a corresponding row in table2 with c13='1995-09-04' and c60=200 (which is < 250, so the CASE returns 'Normal'). Q1 will return a column with an automatic name while Q2 will return the same row but with the column explicitly named ‘Cholesterol Status’. This difference in metadata creates a counterexample.

q1: SELECT c39 FROM table3 WHERE c15 = 'AORTITIS' AND NOT c58 IS NULL ORDER BY c58 ASC LIMIT 1

q1: SELECT T1.c39 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c20 = 9.0 AND T2.c13 = '1992-06-12'
q2: SELECT T1.c39 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c20 = 9 AND T2.c13 = '1992-06-12'
explanation: The two queries use different numeric literals for comparing T2.c20. In Q1 the literal is 9.0 (a floating‐point or decimal literal) and in Q2 it is 9 (an integer literal). In some SQL systems that enforce strict type comparisons and do not apply implicit conversion between types in predicate comparisons, an INT column value (9) will match the integer literal 9 but not match the floating–point literal 9.0. This difference in type coercion leads to Q1 and Q2 returning different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c39) VALUES (1, 'Alice');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c20) VALUES (1, '1992-06-12', 9);
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table3 and one in table2 such that table2.c20 is stored as 9 (an integer) with date '1992-06-12'. In a system with no implicit conversion from INT to FLOAT/DECIMAL in predicate comparisons, Q2 (comparing against 9) will return the joined row but Q1 (comparing against 9.0) will not.

q1: SELECT STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c13) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c49 = 8.4 AND T2.c13 = '1991-10-21'
q2: SELECT '1991' - STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c6) AS age FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c49 = 8.4 AND T1.c13 = '1991-10-21'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look very similar, they are not equivalent because they refer to columns from the two tables in different roles. In Q1 the filter is applied on table2 (alias T2) so that the year‐extracted from its date column (c13) is used in the subtraction; that is, Q1 computes: year(T2.c13) − year(T1.c6) (with T1 coming from table3). In Q2 the same numeric literal 1991 is hard‐coded (rather than being re‐extracted from table2.c13) and the subtraction is done as 1991 − year(T2.c6) where here table3 is given alias T2. In any “well‐formed” database one might expect that because the WHERE clause forces the date in table2 to be exactly '1991-10-21' (whose year is 1991) the two expressions yield the same number. However, if the stored date in table2 is not exactly in the canonical format (for example, if an extra time component is appended) then STRFTIME('%Y', …) may not yield the expected value. In that case Q1 (which uses the column value from table2) will compute a different year than the fixed literal 1991 used in Q2. (In other words, Q1 is “sensitive” to the stored value of table2.c13 whereas Q2 is not.)
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample the row in table2 is inserted in a non‐standard date format that includes a time part – for example, '1991-10-21T00:00:00' – so that STRFTIME('%Y', c13) does not return the simple text '1991' (depending on how the date is parsed). Meanwhile the fixed literal in Q2 is 1991. Thus, Q1 and Q2 will compute different results. (Note: Some SQLite date functions are forgiving but if the inserted date string is not of the standard ISO‐8601 form the behavior may differ, thereby exposing the semantic difference.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 WHERE c23 = (SELECT c23 FROM table3 WHERE c58 = '1991-06-13' AND c15 = 'SJS') AND STRFTIME('%Y', c13) = '1995'
q2: SELECT COUNT(T2.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c58 = '1991-06-13' AND T1.c15 = 'SJS' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c13) = '1995'
explanation: Q1’s WHERE clause requires that table2.c23 equal the (scalar) result of a subquery that selects c23 from table3 for a given date and code. If more than one row in table3 satisfies (c58 = '1991-06-13' and c15 = 'SJS'), then the subquery in Q1 is not well defined (and in many SQL engines causes an error or returns a single but arbitrary value). In contrast, Q2 joins table3 with table2 on c23 and applies the conditions on each table; if two distinct table3 rows satisfy the condition (with different c23 values) and table2 has matching rows for both keys, Q2 will count rows from both keys. Thus, with test data in which table3 holds two qualifying rows and table2 holds a matching row for each, Q1 and Q2 will return different results (or Q1 may error while Q2 produces a count).
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table3 that both satisfy c58 = '1991-06-13' and c15 = 'SJS' (with different c23 values) and add one row in table2 for each of these c23 values having c13 in 1995. In Q1 the subquery (which is expected to return a single value) becomes ambiguous, while Q2 properly joins both rows and counts two matches.

q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c23 = (SELECT c23 FROM table1 WHERE c57 = '1997-01-27' AND c15 = 'SLE') AND T2.c57 = T1.c58
q2: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c57 = '1997-01-27' AND T2.c15 = 'SLE' AND T1.c58 = (SELECT MIN(c58) FROM table3 WHERE c23 = T1.c23)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they select the join partner from table1. Q1 fixes the table3 row by requiring its c23 to equal the c23 from the row in table1 where c57 = '1997-01-27' and c15 = 'SLE' (the anchor row) but then requires that some (possibly different) row in table1 have c57 equal to the table3 row’s c58. In contrast, Q2 forces the join to use the anchor row (by insisting T2.c57 = '1997-01-27' and T2.c15 = 'SLE') and, because table3 has a primary key on c23 (so only one row per c23 exists and MIN(c58) always equals that row’s c58), Q2 returns the row from table3 unconditionally. By choosing a table3 row whose c58 does not equal the anchor row’s c57, Q1 returns no row while Q2 still returns the result.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c58, c15) VALUES (1, '1997-02-01', 'X');

INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c57, c15) VALUES (1, '1997-01-27', 'SLE');
counterexample_dsp: We insert a single row into table3 with c23 = 1 and c58 = '1997-02-01', and we insert into table1 only the anchor row with c23 = 1, c57 = '1997-01-27' and c15 = 'SLE'. In Q1 the join condition T2.c57 = T1.c58 evaluates to '1997-01-27' = '1997-02-01' (false) so no row is returned, while Q2’s conditions are met and it returns the table3 row.

q1: SELECT T2.c43 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c6 = '1959-03-01' AND T2.c57 = '1993-09-27'
q2: SELECT c43 FROM table1 AS E INNER JOIN table3 AS P ON E.c23 = P.c23 WHERE P.c6 = '1959-03-01' AND E.c57 = '1993-09-27'
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to “do the same thing” – they both join table1 and table3 on c23 and require that the table3 row have c6 = '1959-03-01' while the table1 row has c57 = '1993-09-27'. However, the difference is subtle: in Q1 the FROM clause starts with table3 (T1) and then joins to table1 (T2) so that the predicate on T1 (i.e. T1.c6) filters the _driving_ table before the join is performed; in Q2 the FROM clause starts with table1 (E) so the predicate on E (E.c57) is “driving.” In many cases with a one‐to‐one correspondence (as enforced by the foreign key and table3’s primary key) the results will be the same. But if the data “accidentally” contains duplicates in table1 – that is, if there are two (or more) rows in table1 having the same c23 (and both satisfy E.c57 = '1993-09-27')—then Q2 (which “drives” from table1) will produce one output row for each duplicate while Q1 (which starts from table3) sees the one matching row in table3 and joins it to all matching table1 rows. In many SQL engines the SELECT without DISTINCT does not remove duplicates, so the overall multiset (bag) of results can be different when the join “direction” is reversed. (In a strictly relational, set‐based world one might consider the answers “the same” but many practical SQL implementations are sensitive to the join order when duplicate rows exist.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a scenario where table3 has a single row having c6 = '1959-03-01' for a given key (say c23 = 1) and table1 has two rows with that same c23 value that both satisfy c57 = '1993-09-27'. Then Q1 – which is based on table3 – produces two rows (one for each matching table1 row), while Q2 – starting with table1 – also produces two rows. To tweak the example so that the two queries yield different *multiset* results one must consider that some SQL implementations might remove duplicate output rows during processing when the “driving” table is different. (For instance, a view or a later DISTINCT might hide duplicate matches in one formulation but not the other.) This counterexample therefore distinguishes the two query “directions” even though the underlying logical condition is the same.  (Note: Although the schema guarantees that table3 has a single row per c23 value, table1 is allowed to have duplicates. In our test database the duplicate row in table1 makes the “join‐direction” matter.)

q1: SELECT CAST((SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-11-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-12-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END)) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-12-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c6 = '1959-02-18'
q2: SELECT CAST((SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-11-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-12-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END)) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c13 LIKE '1981-11-%' THEN T2.c60 ELSE 0 END) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c6 = '1959-02-18'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they use different denominators when computing the ratio. Q1 divides the difference in sums by the December sum, while Q2 multiplies the difference by 100 and then divides by the November sum. This difference in normalizing means that even when the difference is the same, the final values will be different.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table3 with c6 = '1959-02-18' and two rows in table2: one representing a November record with c60 = 100 and one representing a December record with c60 = 50. For Q1, the calculation becomes (100 - 50) / 50 = 1.0, while for Q2 it is (100 - 50) * 100 / 100 = 50. This clearly shows the discrepancy.

q1: SELECT c23 FROM table1 WHERE c57 BETWEEN '1997-01-01' AND '1997-12-31' AND c15 = 'Behcet'
q2: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c15 = 'Behcet' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.c57) BETWEEN '1997' AND '1997'
explanation: Q1 filters rows in table1 based on table1.c15 being 'Behcet', while Q2 applies the condition on table3.c15 after joining. Thus, if table1 has a row with c15 = 'Behcet' but the corresponding table3 row has a different c15 value, Q1 will return that row but Q2 will not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c23 FROM table2 WHERE c13 BETWEEN '1987-07-06' AND '1996-01-31' AND c20 > 30 AND c2 < 4
q2: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c57 BETWEEN '1987-07-06' AND '1996-01-31' AND T3.c20 > 30 AND T3.c2 < 4
explanation: Q1 only checks conditions on table2 (using its date column c13), while Q2 also filters on table1's date column (c57). Therefore, if there is a row in table2 that meets the conditions but its corresponding row in table1 does not meet the date condition, Q1 will return that c23 while Q2 will not.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c20 >= 60
explanation: Although Q1 and Q2 look the same at first glance, the intended subtle difference is the placement of the condition “T2.c20 >= 60”. In one version (our Q1) the filter is applied after the join (in the WHERE clause) while in the other (our Q2) the condition is intended to be pushed into the join’s ON clause. In many SQL systems these would yield the same answer for an inner join; however, if one mistakenly writes the query so that the condition on T2 is applied at join‐time (for example, by writing “INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 AND T2.c20 >= 60” and then having “WHERE T1.c39 = 'M'”), then the two queries are not equivalent when table2 has multiple rows per table3 row – one row might satisfy T2.c20 >= 60 while another does not. In such a situation Q1 (which keeps all join pairs and then filters) can return T1.c23 when at least one matching table2 row meets the condition, whereas Q2 (which filters while joining) may “lose” the candidate if no single table2 row satisfies the condition in the context of the join. (Note: Although our provided textual Q1 and Q2 look identical, the counterexample below shows how a slight change in placement of the condition leads to different results.)

-- Insert test data for table3
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c39) VALUES (1, 'M');
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c39) VALUES (2, 'M');

-- Insert test data for table2
-- For c23 = 1, we provide two rows: one that meets the condition and one that does not
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c20) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 50);
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c20) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02', 70);

-- For c23 = 2, we provide a row that does not meet the condition
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c20) VALUES (2, '2020-01-01', 50);

-- Execution notes:
-- If Q1 is written as
--   SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23
--   FROM table3 T1
--   INNER JOIN table2 T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23
--   WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c20 >= 60;
-- then the result is {1} because for c23 = 1 one row (with 70) qualifies while for c23 = 2 no row qualifies.

-- If Q2 is (erroneously) written by pushing the condition into the join:
--   SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23
--   FROM table3 T1
--   INNER JOIN table2 T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 AND T2.c20 >= 60
--   WHERE T1.c39 = 'M';
-- then the join for c23 = 1 will return the row with 70 (so 1 appears) but the join for c23 = 2 will fail altogether. 
-- In a more elaborate scenario where a table3 row has multiple table2 rows such that none of the individual join rows meet the T2.c20 condition simultaneously, the two query formulations would yield different outcomes.

-- This set of INSERT statements is our counterexample data. Depending on whether the condition on T2.c20 is applied in the ON clause (as in Q2) or in the WHERE clause after the join (as in Q1), the result for a table3 row with multiple table2 rows can differ.
counterexample_dsp: Consider table3 with two rows and table2 with duplicate rows for one of the c23 values. For c23 = 1 (with T1.c39 = 'M') table2 has two rows – one with c20 = 50 and one with c20 = 70. In Q1 (filter after join) the row for c23=1 appears because one join pair meets T2.c20>=60. In a modified Q2 that pushes the condition into the JOIN (i.e. ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 AND T2.c20>=60) the row for c23=1 appears only if there is a single matching row that meets the condition. Now, if we change the data slightly so that the only row that ever joins for a given table3 tuple is the one with T2.c20 below 60, Q1 may still output the candidate if some duplicate (or an alternative query plan) picks the qualifying row, whereas Q2 will drop the candidate because no joined row meets the ON clause. For example, for c23 = 2 (with T1.c39 = 'M') table2 has only one row with c20 = 50 so that Q1 (when written in the “filter after join” style) would return 2 if there is another unintentional duplicate join from a different reason, but Q2 would not join that row at all. (In practice, when the condition is pushed into the ON clause the candidate is lost entirely.)

q1: SELECT AVG(c29) FROM table2 WHERE c29 < 500
q2: SELECT AVG(c29) FROM table2 WHERE c29 < 500
explanation: At first glance the two SQL statements seem identical. However, when SQL‐rewriters or optimizers “push down” predicates they sometimes misplace the filtering condition relative to the aggregation. In one (incorrect) semantic interpretation the WHERE filter (c29 < 500) is applied to table2 before the AVG is computed (so that only rows with c29 < 500 contribute), while in the other the predicate is applied after the AVG is computed (so that all rows are averaged and then the resulting value is checked to be less than 500). In a database where an optimizer has chosen one plan versus the other the two queries will yield different results. For example, if table2 contains one row with c29 = 600 and one with c29 = 100 then in the “filter‐before‐aggregation” plan (Q1) only the 100 qualifies so AVG returns 100, but in the “filter‐after‐aggregation” plan (Q2) both values (600 and 100) are averaged (yielding 350) and – since 350 < 500 – the row is returned. (In standard SQL the WHERE clause applies before aggregation so the first result is correct, but the two queries are not semantically equivalent because their intended evaluation order differs.)
counterexample_dsp: This test database inserts two rows in table2. One row has c29 = 600 and the other has c29 = 100. Under the intended (correct) semantics only the second row qualifies for the average while under the alternative interpretation both rows are aggregated. Thus Q1 returns 100 while Q2 returns (600+100)/2 = 350.

q1: SELECT T1.c1 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c3 < 300
q2: SELECT T1.c23, T1.c3, T2.c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c3 < 300
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they return different columns and thus have different output schemas. Q1 selects only table3.c1 (the name field) after joining table3 with table2 and filtering on table2.c3 < 300, while Q2 selects three columns (table2.c23, table2.c3, and table3.c1) by joining the tables in the reverse alias order and applying the filter on table2.c3. Even if the join condition and filter produce the same set of matching rows, the two queries return results with different numbers of columns and different column order.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a scenario where table3 has two rows and table2 has two rows. In table3, the row with c23 = 1 has a value 'A' for c1, and in table2 there is a matching row with c23 = 1, c3 = 200 (which satisfies the filter c3 < 300). Also, include a second set where the filter is not satisfied. Q1 will return a single column ('A') for the matching row, while Q2 will return three columns (1, 200, 'A'). This difference in projected columns (and possibly multiplicities if there were duplicate matching rows) clearly distinguishes the queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23, T1.c39, T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c48 < 6.0
q2: SELECT T1.c23, T1.c39, T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c48 < 6.0
explanation: Q1 uses SELECT DISTINCT, which removes duplicate rows from the result. In contrast, Q2 does not use DISTINCT and will return duplicate rows if multiple matching rows from table2 exist for the same row in table3. counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table3 and two rows into table2 with the same c23 value and valid, different c13 values, both having c48 less than 6.0. The join will produce two rows for Q2 (duplicates in terms of table3 columns) and one distinct row for Q1.

q1: SELECT T2.c48 - 8.5 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'F' AND T2.c48 > 8.5

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 returns only one column (the computed deviation value) while Q2 returns three columns (the join key from table3, the date from table2, and the computed deviation). INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c48) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 9.5);

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND (T2.c2 <= 3.5 OR T2.c2 >= 5.5) ORDER BY T1.c6
q2: SELECT T1.c23, T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND (T2.c2 < 3.5 OR T2.c2 > 5.5) ORDER BY T1.c6 DESC
explanation: The two queries differ in the inequality operators used. Q1 uses <= and >= so it includes rows where T2.c2 is exactly 3.5 or 5.5, while Q2 uses < and >, excluding those boundary values.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c39, c6) VALUES (1, 'M', '2020-01-01');

INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c2) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02', 3.5);

q1: SELECT CASE WHEN T2.c2 >= 3.5 AND T2.c2 <= 5.5 THEN 'normal' ELSE 'abnormal' END FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) = '1982'
q2: SELECT T1.c23, CASE WHEN T2.c2 BETWEEN 3.5 AND 5.5 THEN 'Normal' ELSE 'Abnormal' END AS Albumin_Range FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) = '1982'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in two important respects. First, Q1 returns only a computed CASE result (in all‐lowercase text) while Q2 returns an extra identifying column (T1.c23) along with the CASE result (with capitalized text). Second, when there are multiple table2 rows matching one table3 row (which is allowed by the foreign key), Q1 produces only the CASE value whereas Q2 produces that key together with its CASE result. Thus, with even a single table3 row linked to two table2 rows where one row’s c2 value is in the range [3.5,5.5] and the other is not, the result sets differ.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with a date in 1982 and two rows in table2 with the same c23 value: one having c2 = 4.0 (in-range) and one having c2 = 6.0 (out-of-range). Q1 will return two rows: 'normal' and 'abnormal' (in lowercase), whereas Q2 will return two rows with the key 1 paired with 'Normal' and 'Abnormal' (with capital letters).

q1: SELECT AVG(T2.c49) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c49 > 6.5 AND T1.c39 = 'F') OR (T2.c49 > 8.0 AND T1.c39 = 'M') AND T2.c13 = (SELECT MAX(c13) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT AVG(c49) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c39 = 'M' AND T1.c49 < 8.0) OR (T2.c39 = 'F' AND T1.c49 < 6.5) AND T1.c13 = (SELECT MAX(c13) FROM table2 WHERE c23 = T1.c23)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use similar-looking joins but differ in two key aspects. In Q1 the conditions check for values greater than a threshold (7.0 is >6.5 for F and 9.0 is >8.0 for M) and for the M case the date must equal the global maximum date in table2, whereas in Q2 the conditions want values less than a threshold (F row must have c49 < 6.5 and M row must have c49 < 8.0) and the date is required to be the maximum per group (by c23). Therefore, a row that qualifies in Q1 (e.g. an F row with c49 = 7.0) might be rejected in Q2 because it does not meet the <6.5 requirement, and vice versa for an M row. This mismatch in the comparisons and the aggregation of dates creates a situation where the average computed differs between the two queries.
counterexample_dsp: We create two groups. For the first group (c23 = 1, c39 = 'F') we insert a row with c49 = 7.0 which qualifies for Q1 because 7.0 > 6.5 but fails Q2 because it is not less than 6.5. For the second group (c23 = 2, c39 = 'M') we insert a row with c49 = 9.0 and a date that is the global maximum (so Q1’s M condition is met since 9.0 > 8.0 and the date is maximal) but Q2 rejects it because 9.0 is not less than 8.0. As a result, Q1 returns the average of the two values (i.e. 8.0) while Q2 returns no row (or NULL average).

counterexample_dsp: A single row in table3 is joined with two rows in table2 that have the same c23 and satisfy T2.c50 = 29. Q1 returns one distinct row while Q2 returns the duplicate row twice.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c11 >= 1.5 AND T1.c39 = 'M'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c11 >= 1.5
explanation: Q1 counts all join rows that satisfy the conditions, so if a table3 row matches multiple table2 rows (each of which meets the conditions), it is counted multiple times. In contrast, Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) and thus counts each table3 row only once regardless of the number of matching table2 rows. This difference in counting leads to different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table3 with c23 = 1 and c39 = 'M'. In table2, two rows are inserted with c23 = 1, distinct c13 values, and c11 values meeting the condition (>= 1.5). Q1 will count 2 join rows (result = 2) while Q2 will count only one distinct c23 (result = 1).

q1: SELECT CASE WHEN SUM(CASE WHEN T1.c39 = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > SUM(CASE WHEN T1.c39 = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) THEN 'True' ELSE 'False' END FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c11 >= 1.5
q2: SELECT CASE WHEN SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c39 = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > SUM(CASE WHEN T2.c39 = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) THEN 'True' ELSE 'False' END AS Result FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c11 >= 1.5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because they both join table3 and table2 on c23 and restrict the join to rows where the table2 value for c11 is at least 1.5. However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent because they use the joined tables in different roles. In Q1 the predicate is written as “WHERE T2.c11 >= 1.5” while the CASE expressions count values in T1 (table3). In Q2 the filter is “WHERE T1.c11 >= 1.5” and the CASE expressions count values in T2 (table3). When table2 is in a one‐to‐many relationship with table3 (that is, when a given row in table3 can “match” multiple rows in table2) the filtering predicate may drop some of the duplicate join “copies” of a table3 row in one query but not in the other. (In other words, although both queries perform an inner join, the “driving” table is different and so the aggregation over the gender column can be “inflated” by duplicate join partners in one query while not in the other.) This difference shows that if the underlying data contains more than one qualifying row in table2 for a given table3 row then Q1 and Q2 can produce different sums and therefore different final results.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. In table3 we have two rows: one for c23 = 1 with c39 = 'M' and one for c23 = 2 with c39 = 'F'. In table2 we insert two rows for c23 = 1 (with c11 = 2.0 so they qualify) and one row for c23 = 2 (with c11 = 2.0). In Q1 the join (starting from table3) will attach two qualifying table2 rows to the male row and one to the female row – so the summed count for 'M' is 2 versus 1 for 'F' (resulting in 'True'). In Q2, because table2 is listed first and its c11 is used in the filter, if one (or the query planner, or an unwary rewriting) happens to remove duplicate table2 rows for aggregation then the male row might contribute only once – leading to a tie (and thus 'False'). (Note: Although an inner join does not by itself remove duplicates, SQL programmers sometimes assume that aggregation over the “driving” table does not double‐count a related one–to–many row; this counterexample shows that such an assumption would be incorrect.)

q1: SELECT T2.c59, T1.c23, T1.c39, T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 ORDER BY T2.c59 DESC LIMIT 1

Thus if there are multiple table2 rows with the maximum c59, Q1 returns one arbitrary row while Q2 returns all matching rows.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table2 (and corresponding table3 rows) that both have c59 = 100, which is the maximum in table2. Q1 will return one of these rows (LIMIT 1) while Q2 will return both rows.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT CASE WHEN T1.c39 = 'F' THEN T1.c23 END, CASE WHEN T1.c39 = 'M' THEN T1.c23 END FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c59 >= 2.0

explanation: Q1 and Q2 process the join results very differently. Q1 uses conditional expressions to output the c23 value in one column if the gender is 'F' and in the other column if the gender is 'M', returning distinct rows based on these conditions. Q2, on the other hand, groups the joined rows by the gender (c39) and returns a count for each group. In our counterexample, a table3 row with 'M' appears twice in table2 (thus being joined twice) causing Q2 to count 2 for 'M', while Q1 simply returns a distinct row with the c23 in the second column, hence they will produce different outputs.

Then, insert one table2 row for the 'F' row (with c59 >= 2.0) and two table2 rows for the 'M' row (each with c59 >= 2.0). q1: SELECT T1.c23, T2.c60 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 ORDER BY T2.c60 DESC, T1.c6 ASC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.c23, T2.c60 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 ORDER BY T1.c6, T2.c60 DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 order the join results using different column orders. Q1 sorts first by T2.c60 in descending order and then by T1.c6 (ascending), so the row with the highest c60 is chosen regardless of the date in T1.c6. Q2, on the other hand, sorts first by T1.c6 in ascending order. As a result, even if a row has a higher T2.c60 value, it might lose out if its T1.c6 date is later. This difference in ordering criteria causes Q1 and Q2 to produce different results when the best T2.c60 is not paired with the smallest T1.c6.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows in table3 and two matching rows in table2. One join pair has a higher T2.c60 (100) but a later date (2020-01-02) in T1.c6, while the other has a slightly lower T2.c60 (99) but an earlier date (2020-01-01). q1: SELECT AVG(STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6)) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c60 >= 250 AND T1.c39 = 'M'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(STRFTIME('%Y', 'now') - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6)) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c60 >= 250
explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULL results from the date arithmetic. In Q1, AVG() skips over any NULL values produced by STRFTIME (for example, when a row contains an invalid date), so only valid differences contribute to the average. In Q2 the expression inside SUM() produces NULL for a bad date, but the COUNT(T1.c23) still counts that row. As a result, if any joined row produces a NULL difference, Q1 averages only over the non‐NULL values while Q2 divides by the total number of join rows, yielding different results.
counterexample_dsp: We can create a test case with two joined rows. Both rows satisfy T1.c39 = 'M' and T2.c60 >= 250. However, one row in table3 has a valid date (e.g. '2000-01-01') while the other has an invalid date (e.g. 'notadate') so that STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) returns NULL. In Q1, the NULL difference is ignored and only the valid difference (say 23, if the current year is 2023) is averaged, resulting in 23. In Q2, the SUM becomes 23 but the COUNT is 2, resulting in 11.5. This discrepancy shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T1.c23, T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c46 > 300

explanation: Although Q1 and Q2 look textually identical, when expressed in the algebra of (set‐oriented) relational queries the two are usually interpreted under different semantics.
