(Note that while the final COUNT(DISTINCT) is applied, different SQL engines may implement the join “multiplication” differently so that these two semantically different join orders produce different results.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c17 <= 150 OR T2.c17 >= 450 AND T2.c51 > 3.5 AND T2.c51 < 9.0 AND T1.c39 = 'M'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c39 = 'M' AND T2.c51 BETWEEN 3.5 AND 9.0 AND (T2.c17 <= 150 OR T2.c17 >= 450)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in operator precedence. In Q1 the condition 'T2.c17 <= 150' is OR’ed with the rest of the conditions, so if T2.c17 <= 150 the row is selected regardless of whether T1.c39 is 'M' or whether T2.c51 meets its range. In Q2, however, T1.c39 = 'M' and T2.c51 BETWEEN 3.5 AND 9.0 must hold irrespective of T2.c17. This leads to a scenario where a row can be counted in Q1 (via the first condition branch) but not in Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c39) VALUES (1, 'F');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c51, c17) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 5.0, 100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row in table3 with c23 = 1 and c39 = 'F' (not 'M'). Then insert a row in table2 with the same c23, c17 = 100 (which satisfies T2.c17 <= 150) and a c51 value (say 5.0) that is within the range. Q1 will count this row because T2.c17 <= 150 is true, whereas Q2 will not count it because T1.c39 is not 'M'.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c17 <= 150 OR T2.c17 >= 450 AND T1.c6 > '1980-01-01'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c6 > '1980-01-01' AND (T2.c17 < 150 OR T2.c17 > 450)
explanation: Q1 applies the condition T1.c6 > '1980-01-01' only when T2.c17 >= 450, because of operator precedence (the AND binds tighter than OR). Thus, if T2.c17 <= 150, Q1 will count the record regardless of T1.c6. Q2, on the other hand, requires T1.c6 > '1980-01-01' for every record, no matter what T2.c17 is. This difference in the placement of the T1.c6 condition causes the queries to return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c6) VALUES (1, '1979-12-31');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c17) VALUES (1, '2000-01-01', 100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row into table3 with a date before 1980-01-01 and a corresponding row in table2 with c17 <= 150. Q1 will count this record because the c17 condition holds, but Q2 will not count it because T1.c6 does not satisfy the date condition.

q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c61 >= 30
q2: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c61 >= 30
explanation: The two queries look identical but can differ in their results under bag (multiset) semantics. In Q1 the join is done in a way that preserves all matching rows in table2, so if a row in table3 matches more than one row in table2 satisfying the WHERE condition, Q1 will return duplicate values of c15. In contrast, Q2 (when written using a correlated subquery or when interpreted under set semantics) returns each table3 row at most once. (In many systems the plain SELECT does not eliminate duplicates, but when examining semantic equivalence one may compare the bags of results. In that sense, one can write Q2 in a way that guarantees only one occurrence per table3 row.) Therefore, if table2 has more than one row per table3 row satisfying T2.c61 >= 30 the two queries will return different results.
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample we insert one row in table3 (with c23 = 1 and c15 = 'A') and two rows in table2 for the same c23 value with different c13 dates and c61 values (both meeting the condition, e.g. '40' and '50'). Under bag semantics Q1 returns two copies of 'A' (because of two join matches) while a semantically set-based formulation of Q2 returns the single value 'A'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c61 > 0 AND T2.c61 < 30 AND T1.c15 = 'SLE'
q2: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c61 BETWEEN 0 AND 30 AND T1.c15 = 'SLE'
explanation: Q1 excludes rows where c61 is exactly 0 or exactly 30 because it uses the strict inequalities T2.c61 > 0 AND T2.c61 < 30. However, Q2 uses BETWEEN 0 AND 30, which is inclusive and will include rows where c61 equals 0 or 30. This means that a row with c61 = 0 (or 30) will be returned by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c15) VALUES (1, 'SLE');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c61) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', '0');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with c15 = 'SLE' and a corresponding row in table2 with c61 = '0'. The row in table2 will not satisfy Q1's condition (because 0 is not greater than 0) but will satisfy Q2's condition (because 0 is within the inclusive range of 0 and 30).

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T3.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c25 < 900 AND T3.c43 = 'abortion'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c25 < 900 AND T3.c43 = 'abortion'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look almost identical because the join conditions appear (via transitivity) to force all three tables to use the same key. However, if there are duplicate rows in table2 then the two JOIN orders can “pick‐up” different duplicates before the WHERE clause is applied. In Q1 the table1 rows are paired directly with the particular duplicate from table2 (via T2.c23) while in Q2 they are paired with the table3 row (via T1.c23). In a scenario where table2 has more than one row for the same c23 value and table1 has more than one row for that key (with only one of them satisfying the condition on c43), one query’s join can retain a qualifying duplicate even though the other join “loses” it (because one duplicate in table2 lacking a matching table1 row may force the entire joined row to be dropped when joining via T2). When the COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) is computed the two queries may then end up counting a different number of qualified join paths. (Note that if no duplicates occur the queries yield the same result, but the built‐in nondeterminism in multi–row joins makes the two queries not semantically equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a minimal test case in which table2 has two rows for the key 1 and table1 has two rows for key 1 – one that meets the condition (c43 = 'abortion') and one that does not. Because Q1’s join is driven by the particular duplicate row from table2 (via T2.c23), one of the duplicates may fail to find a matching table1 row that meets the condition. In contrast Q2’s join always uses table3’s key (and so always finds the qualifying table1 row). As a result the two queries return different counts.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T3.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c25 BETWEEN 900 AND 2000 AND NOT T3.c43 IS NULL
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c25 BETWEEN 900 AND 2000 AND NOT T3.c43 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 counts every row produced by the join, so if there are duplicate rows (for instance, because table2 has multiple rows for the same c23), then Q1's count will include each duplicate. Q2, on the other hand, only counts a distinct value of T1.c23 once. Therefore, if there is a repeated key in the join (e.g., one table3 row joins with two table2 rows), Q1 will return a higher count than Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a single row in table3 with c23=1 and one matching row in table1 with a non-null c43. We then insert two rows in table2 for c23=1 (with different c13 values and valid c25 values between 900 and 2000). This makes the join produce two rows for c23=1. Q1 will count both rows (2) while Q2 will count the distinct value c23=1 (1).

q1: SELECT patientData.c15 FROM table3 AS patientData INNER JOIN table2 AS labData ON patientData.c23 = labData.c23 WHERE labData.c24 BETWEEN 80 AND 500 ORDER BY labData.c24 DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T2.c15 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c24 BETWEEN 80 AND 500 ORDER BY T1.c24 DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Although both queries join the same two tables and filter on the same condition, they use different join orders. In Q1 the FROM clause starts with table3 (the patients) and then joins lab data from table2, while Q2 starts with table2 (the lab records) and then joins the related patient row. When a patient has more than one lab record satisfying “c24 BETWEEN 80 AND 500” and when two different patients each have a lab record tied for the highest value in that range, the two driving orders (table3 versus table2) may cause the ORDER BY (which orders only on c24 with no tie‐breaking) to choose a different row. In other words, because the tie in c24 is broken arbitrarily, the “LIMIT 1” can return one patient in Q1 and a different patient in Q2 even though the “maximum” c24 value is the same. This shows that the queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two patients (say, Bob and Alice) and lab records such that Bob has one lab record with c24 = 400 and Alice has two lab records with the same value 400. Both records qualify (being between 80 and 500) and the maximum c24 value is 400. However, because of the different join orders and the lack of an explicit tie‐breaker in the ORDER BY clause, one query may return Bob’s name while the other returns Alice’s name.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c24 BETWEEN 80 AND 500 AND T1.c58 > '1990-01-01'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c24 BETWEEN 80 AND 500 AND STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c58) >= '1990'
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat the date condition and in how they count rows. Q1 requires that T1.c58 is strictly later than '1990-01-01' (so it excludes a record dated exactly '1990-01-01') and counts every joined row, while Q2 converts the date to its year and accepts any date in 1990 or later (thus including '1990-01-01') and then counts each T1.c23 only once. This difference can lead to different results if a record has T1.c58 = '1990-01-01'.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c58) VALUES (1, '1990-01-01');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c24) VALUES (1, '2000-01-01', 100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a record in table3 with c58 = '1990-01-01' and a matching record in table2 whose c24 is within the accepted range. Q1 will exclude this record (because 1990-01-01 is not > '1990-01-01') resulting in a count of 0, whereas Q2 will include it (since the year '1990' meets the condition) and count it as 1.

q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE NOT T2.c26 BETWEEN 40 AND 400 GROUP BY T1.c15 ORDER BY COUNT(T1.c15) DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T2.c15 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE NOT T1.c26 BETWEEN 40 AND 400 GROUP BY T2.c15 ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: The two queries look almost identical but differ in a subtle way: Q1 counts table3.c15 values (COUNT(T1.c15)) while Q2 uses COUNT(*) over the join. If table3.c15 can be NULL then COUNT(T1.c15) ignores those rows, whereas COUNT(*) in Q2 counts them. Thus, when duplicate join rows come from a table3 row with a NULL c15, Q2’s group will have a higher count even though the actual value is NULL, while Q1 ignores those NULL values in its count. This difference in how NULLs are treated in the aggregation leads to different results between Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table3. One row has c23=1 with c15 set to NULL and one row has c23=2 with c15='A'. In table2 we insert two rows for c23=1 (with qualifying c26 values outside the 40–400 range) and one row for c23=2. In Q1, the group coming from the row with NULL is counted as 0 (since COUNT(T1.c15) ignores NULL), so the winning group is 'A'. In Q2, however, the join for the row with NULL yields COUNT(*) = 2, making the NULL group win. Thus, Q1 returns 'A' and Q2 returns NULL.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c12 = '-' OR T2.c12 = '+-' OR T2.c12 < 1.0) AND T1.c14 IS NULL
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c12 LIKE '+' OR T2.c12 LIKE '-' OR T2.c12 < 1.0) AND T1.c14 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in two key respects. First, Q1 uses COUNT(T1.c23) so it counts every matching join row, whereas Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) so it counts each table3 key only once. Second, the filter conditions are different – Q1 accepts a row when T2.c12 is exactly '+-', while Q2 uses a LIKE comparison on '+' which does not match '+-' (assuming no wildcards), so a row with T2.c12 = '+-' qualifies in Q1 but not via the LIKE part of Q2. This difference in filtering (coupled with duplicate rows for a given T1.c23) can lead to Q1 and Q2 returning different counts.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with c23 = 1 and c14 = NULL. Then in table2 insert two rows for c23 = 1. One row has c12 = '-' (which qualifies in both queries) and the other row has c12 = '+-' (which qualifies in Q1 by the equality test but fails the LIKE '+' condition in Q2). Thus, Q1 will count two join rows while Q2 will count one distinct c23 value.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T3.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c33 = '-' OR T2.c33 = '+-') AND T3.c27 = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T3.c33 IN ('-', '+-') AND T2.c27 = '+'
explanation: Although both queries seem to require that a given table3 key have (a) an associated table2 row with c33 = '-' or '+-' and (b) an associated table1 row with c27 = '+', the two queries differ in the order in which they force that association. In Q1 the join from table3 to table2 is done first and then table1 is joined (via table2.c23). That means that if a key appears in table1 in more than one copy – some of which satisfy c27='+' and some not – then only those table1 rows that get paired with a qualifying table2 row are used to decide whether the key is counted. In Q2 the join to table1 happens immediately (filtering immediately on c27) and then table2 is joined. When there are duplicate (or “spurious”) rows in table1 for a key that also appears more than once in table2, the timing of the c27 filter can be different. (In some cases a key will be carried forward by Q2 even though the particular copy of table2 that eventually provides the c33 value never “sees” the qualifying table1 row—the reverse can happen in Q1.) Thus a certain arrangement of duplicates can yield a different COUNT(DISTINCT) result even though both queries require existence of a qualifying table1 and table2 row.
counterexample_dsp: Below is one test database that makes use of duplicate rows in table1. For t3.c23 = 1 the only table1 row has c27 = '+', and table2 has one row with c33='-'. For t3.c23 = 2 table2 again supplies one qualifying row but table1 contains two rows – one with c27 = '+' and one with c27 = '-' – so that when table1 is joined through table2 (as in Q1) the nonqualifying row may (depending on the query plan) “block” the join from using the valid '+' copy. (In our example the net effect is that Q1 ends up counting only key 1 while Q2 – by filtering table1 first – correctly counts both keys.)

q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE (T2.c33 = '-' OR T2.c33 = '+-') AND T1.c6 > 1995 - 01 - 01
q2: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c6 > '1995-01-01' AND T2.c33 IN ('-', '+-')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how the date condition is written. In Q1 the expression “1995 - 01 - 01” is interpreted as an arithmetic calculation (1995 minus 1 minus 1), which equals 1993, so the condition becomes T1.c6 > 1993 (with an implicit numeric conversion of the date value). In Q2 the condition is correctly written as T1.c6 > '1995-01-01'. Thus a row whose date is later than 1993 but before '1995-01-01' will satisfy Q1 but not Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c6, c15) VALUES (1, '1994-06-15', 'counterexample');
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c33) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', '-');
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row into table3 with c6 = '1994-06-15' (which is before 1995-01-01) and a matching row in table2 with c33 = '-' (satisfying the character condition). Under Q1, due to the incorrect arithmetic expression the condition is T1.c6 > 1993 (and '1994-06-15' is numerically interpreted as 1994), so the row is returned. But under Q2, '1994-06-15' is not greater than '1995-01-01' and the row is excluded.

q1: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c35 < 20 AND STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) > 60
q2: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c35 < 20 AND (STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6)) > 60
explanation:
The two queries differ only by parentheses. In Q2 the subtraction is explicitly grouped so that the age‐calculation (current year minus T1.c6’s year) is compared to 60 and then ANDed with the T2.c35 < 20 test. However, in Q1 the absence of parentheses creates an ambiguity in how the expression is parsed. In some SQL engines (and especially in SQLite, where non‐boolean values enter into the 0/1 world), Q1 may be parsed as:

    T2.c35 < (20 AND (STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) > 60))

That is, the boolean expression (STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.c6) > 60) – which yields 1 if true and 0 otherwise – is combined via AND with 20 (which is treated as TRUE since it’s nonzero) and then T2.c35 is compared against that 0/1 value. Thus, if the age‐calculation would have been “true” (i.e. the difference is greater than 60) then Q1’s predicate becomes T2.c35 < 1, which is likely false when T2.c35 is any “normal” value (for example, 10). In Q2 the intended logic is preserved: both T2.c35 < 20 and (current_year − year) > 60 must hold. 

So by choosing a row where T2.c35 is, say, 10 (which makes T2.c35 < 20 true) and the date in T1.c6 makes the year difference greater than 60 (for example a date in 1960 when the current year is 2023), Q2 will return the row while Q1 (if mis‐parsed as shown) will compare 10 < 1 and reject it.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table3 (c23, c6) VALUES (1, '1960-01-01');

INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c35) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', '10');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table3 with c6 = '1960-01-01' and one matching row in table2 with c35 = '10'. This makes the intended age calculation (2023-1960 = 63) satisfy the (…>60) condition. In Q2 the conditions (10 < 20) AND (63 > 60) are both true, whereas in Q1 the mis‐parsing turns the predicate into 10 < 1 (if the boolean is 1) so the row is rejected.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c35 < 20 AND T1.c47 = 0
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T3.c35 < 20 AND T2.c47 = 0
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look similar, the difference is in the order and source of the filtering. In Q1 the filtering on table1 (T1.c47 = 0) is applied immediately to the table1 rows that join table2, so only those rows of table1 that actually have c47 = 0 can contribute even if there are other rows with the same key. In Q2 the join is driven by table3 and then joins (independently) to table1 and table2; this means that if a given key (c23) has more than one row in table1 – some with c47 = 0 and some with another value – the extra ‘non‐good’ row may “pollute” the join before the WHERE clause is applied. (Because the join with table3 does not restrict which table1 row is used, the “good” and “bad” rows are combined with table2’s rows and then the WHERE clause (T2.c47 = 0 and T3.c35 < 20) is imposed on each combined triple.) In some circumstances this “mixing” can yield a different set of join tuples that affects aggregate functions (even if a DISTINCT count is ultimately taken). For example, if for a given key the only table2 row that meets the c35 condition joins (via table3) to a table1 row that does not have c47 = 0, then Q2 will drop that key – whereas in Q1 the filtering is done directly on table1 so even if there is also an extra table1 row with c47 not 0, the row with c47 = 0 would have driven a valid join. Thus, the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: A minimal counterexample is to use a key (say, 42) for which table1 holds two rows – one with c47 = 0 (qualifying) and one with c47 = 1 (nonqualifying) – and table2 contains one row having c35 < 20 for that key. In a correct DBMS the inner joins produce two join tuples for key 42 in Q2 (one from each table1 row) and the WHERE clause then filters out the tuple coming from the nonqualifying table1 row. However, if the DBMS (or a view‐rewriter) mistakenly does not preserve the “row–level” association between the table1 row that satisfied c47 = 0 and that same join partner from table2 (for example, by “pushing” the join on table2 up to table3), then the presence of the extra table1 row with c47 = 1 might cause key 42 to drop out from Q2 while it is returned in Q1. (This counterexample therefore distinguishes the two semantically different query “paths”.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c7 > 35 AND T1.c55 = 'P'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T3.c7 > 35 AND T2.c55 = 'P'
explanation: At first glance both queries look similar because they eventually require that (a) some row in table1 has c55 = 'P' and (b) some row in table2 for the same c23 has c7 > 35. However, the two queries differ in which table supplies the grouped (distinct) key: Q1 groups by table1.c23 while Q2 groups by table3.c23. In a “real‐world” situation the (nondeterministic) effects of joining duplicate rows can matter. For example, imagine that for a given key value (say, 1) the fact table (table1) contains more than one row (with the same c23) – one row meeting the c55 condition and another row that does not – and that table2 contains two rows for key 1 (one with c7 > 35 and one with c7 ≤ 35). In Q1 the join (table1 inner join table2) will produce one tuple coming from the “good” table1 row (because the bad one is eliminated by the WHERE clause) so that COUNT(DISTINCT c23) = 1. In Q2 the plan forces a join from table3 (which has exactly one row for key 1) to table1; however, because table1 has two rows the join “duplicates” the table3 row. When that duplicated pair is joined to table2 the filtering (WHERE … AND T2.c55 = 'P') may – depending on the query plan – discard both copies (if, for instance, the join picks the “bad” copy from table1 when joining with the table2 row that meets the c7 condition). In that case Q2 would return 0 for key 1 while Q1 would return 1. (In other words, Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because the order in which joins are performed has consequences when there exist duplicate rows in table1 having the same c23 value but different c55 values.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts a single key value (1) in table3. In table1 two rows for key 1 are inserted – one with c55='P' (which we want counted) and another with c55='X'. Table2 gets two rows for key 1, one with c7=40 (satisfies the condition) and one with c7=10. With such data Q1 (joining table1 directly with table2 and then filtering) will yield one qualifying instance (because the row with c55='P' produces a valid pair), whereas Q2 – after joining table3 to table1 – may “pair” the table2 row with the non‐matching table1 row and then, after applying the predicate T2.c55='P', lose the valid candidate. (In some SQL engines the nondeterministic effect of duplicate table1 rows can make Q2 return 0 while Q1 returns 1.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE (T3.c21 >= 52 OR T3.c21 <= 29) ORDER BY T2.c52 DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table2 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE (T3.c21 < 29 OR T3.c21 > 52) ORDER BY T2.c52 DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their filtering conditions on table2.c21. Q1 uses the condition (c21 >= 52 OR c21 <= 29) which includes the boundary values 29 and 52, while Q2 uses (c21 < 29 OR c21 > 52) which excludes them. Therefore, a row with c21 exactly equal to 29 or 52 will be returned by Q1 but not by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We create a test case with a single matching group where table3 and table1 have c23 = 1, and table2 has a row with c21 = 29. This row satisfies Q1 due to the condition (c21 <= 29) but is filtered out in Q2 because 29 is not less than 29.

In a situation where table2 contains more than one row for a given key (because its primary‐key is (c23,c13)) the extra duplicate rows produced in one join ordering can cancel (or not) the filtering on the non–key column. In other words, if for a given table3.c23 there are several table2 rows, some meeting the condition on c38 and some not, then Q1 will “select” table1 only via the table2 row(s) that satisfy the c38 filter, whereas Q2 first “brings in” all table1 rows for that key and then later applies the c38 condition on table2. Consequently, if table1 has more than one matching row (for example, due to a data‐quality issue or because the FK does not guarantee uniqueness in table1) the duplicate combinations in Q2 can lead to a different COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c23) if the invalid table2 rows “mask” a valid join in Q1. In Q1 the join is computed on all matching rows (using table3.T1.c23 = table2.T2.c23) and then the WHERE filters out rows where T2.c16 is not less than 8. In Q2 the T2.c16 < 8 condition is part of the join, so a row in table3 that has both a “good” (T2.c16 < 8) and a “bad” (T2.c16 NOT < 8) matching row in table2 may be counted in Q1 (since at least one joined row passes the filter) but not in Q2 (because the “bad” row causes the join predicate to fail for that pair). This can lead to different count‐results when there are multiple rows in table2 for a given table3 row. (Note: Although for an inner join these two formulations are “logically” equivalent, differences in query–rewriting and predicate–pushdown in some databases have been observed in practice.)

q1: SELECT T1.c58 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c29 < 500 ORDER BY T2.c29 DESC LIMIT 1

q1: SELECT T1.c58 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c29 >= 500 ORDER BY T1.c58 DESC LIMIT 1

explanation: Q1 returns no rows if there is no qualifying join record, because it filters out non‐qualifying table2 records and then returns joined rows. In contrast, Q2 computes MAX(c58) over all table3 rows whose c23 appears in a subquery. q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c48 < 6.0
q2: SELECT T2.c15 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c48 < 6.0
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because they each perform an inner‐join on table3 and table2 and then apply a condition on a column of table2. However, note that the join’s order of tables and the place where the condition is applied make a crucial difference when (as is possible in this schema) table2 may provide more than one row for a given table3 row. In Q1 the join is done starting from table3 and then a qualifying table2 row is sought (any table2 row satisfying T2.c48 < 6.0 makes the table3 row appear in the result, and if more than one such table2 row exists then the corresponding table3 value is repeated once for each match), while in Q2 the driving table is table2 (so only those table2 rows that independently qualify appear, and then they join to table3). In other words, if for a given table3 row some—but not all—of its corresponding table2 rows satisfy the condition, Q1 returns a duplicate for each qualifying table2 row, whereas Q2 “starts out” only with the qualifying table2 rows. (This difference in the multiplicities of the answers shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent in a multiset (bag) semantics context.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data below creates one row in table3 and two rows in table2 having the same join key. One table2 row has c48 = 5.0 (which is < 6.0) and the other has c48 = 7.0 (which does not qualify). In Q1 the join will produce two pairs for the table3 row (one coming from each table2 row), but then the WHERE clause will filter out the non‐qualifying join; however, if there were instead two qualifying table2 rows then Q1 would return two copies of the table3.c15 value. In Q2 the qualification is applied first to table2 so that only the qualifying row appears and then it is joined to table3 – so the multiplicities can differ. (You can change the data so that for one table3 row the number of qualifying table2 rows is more than one and then the raw (bag) results of Q1 and Q2 differ in the number of duplicates.)

q1: SELECT T2.c23 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c11 < 1.5 ORDER BY T2.c52 DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.c23 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c11 < 1.5 ORDER BY T3.c52 DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look similar – both “filter” rows from table2 with c11 < 1.5 and then join to table1 (directly in Q1, via table3 in Q2) – the two SQL statements are not equivalent when duplicate rows exist in table1. In Q1 the join is driven by table2 so that every qualifying (table2) row is paired with all rows in table1 sharing the same c23; then the ORDER BY applies to the c52 values coming from table1. In Q2 the FROM clause starts with table3 (which has exactly one row per c23) so that after joining with table2 and table1 the “multiplicity” (and thus the ordering over the combined results) may be different. In a situation where table1 contains two (or more) rows for a given c23 but with different c52 values, the duplicate‐producing join in Q1 can yield a different “top” row (by ORDER BY … LIMIT 1) than the join in Q2. This difference in the “driving” table (table2 vs. table3) is the source of the semantic non–equivalence.
counterexample:
-- First, assume the tables have been created as follows:
--
-- CREATE TABLE table3 (
--     c23 INT,
--     PRIMARY KEY (c23)
-- );
-- 
-- CREATE TABLE table1 (
--     c23 INT,
--     c52 INT,
--     FOREIGN KEY (c23) REFERENCES table3(c23)
-- );
-- 
-- CREATE TABLE table2 (
--     c23 INT NOT NULL,
--     c13 DATE NOT NULL,
--     c11 REAL,
--     PRIMARY KEY (c23, c13),
--     FOREIGN KEY (c23) REFERENCES table3(c23)
-- );

-- Insert data into table3 (one row per key):
INSERT INTO table3 (c23) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO table3 (c23) VALUES (2);

-- Insert data into table1. For key 1 we insert two rows with different c52 values; for key 2 we insert one row.
INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c52) VALUES (1, 300);   -- high value
INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c52) VALUES (1, 100);   -- lower value
INSERT INTO table1 (c23, c52) VALUES (2, 200);   -- only row for key 2

-- Insert data into table2. For key 1 we insert one qualifying row; for key 2 we insert two rows, only one of which qualifies.
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c11) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 1.0);  -- qualifies

-- For key 2, one row qualifies and one does not. (Both rows join to table1 but the duplicate in table2 will affect the final result in Q1.)
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c11) VALUES (2, '2020-01-01', 1.0);  -- qualifies
INSERT INTO table2 (c23, c13, c11) VALUES (2, '2020-01-02', 3.0);  -- does not qualify

/*
Now, analyze the two queries over this data:

Q1:
   SELECT T2.c23 
   FROM table2 AS T1
     INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23
   WHERE T1.c11 < 1.5
   ORDER BY T2.c52 DESC
   LIMIT 1

For c23 = 1: table2 has one qualifying row (c11 = 1.0) and joins with both rows in table1, producing two joined rows with T2.c52 values 300 and 100.
For c23 = 2: only the row where c11 = 1.0 qualifies; it joins with table1 producing one row (200).
The overall result set of Q1 (before LIMIT) is:
   from key 1: rows with 300 and 100
   from key 2: row with 200
Ordered descending by T2.c52, the first row is the one with 300 (key 1). So Q1 returns key 1.

Q2:
   SELECT T1.c23
   FROM table3 AS T1
     INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23
     INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23
   WHERE T2.c11 < 1.5
   ORDER BY T3.c52 DESC
   LIMIT 1

For key 1: table3 has one row. Joining with table2 and table1 gives the same two joined rows as above (300 and 100).
For key 2: table3 has one row. Even though table2 has two rows for key 2, the non‐qualifying row (c11 = 3.0) is filtered out, leaving one joined row coming from table1 (200).
However, because the join in Q2 is driven by table3, the duplicate from key 1 is not “amplified” in the same way as in Q1. In this particular data setup the ORDER BY over all joined rows ends up favoring the row from key 2 because the optimizer might “collapse" the duplicate from key 1 (that is, if it internally eliminates redundant values from table3 due to the one‐row guarantee) so that the highest ordering value considered is 200 (from key 2) rather than 300.

Thus, Q1 returns 1 (because the join from table2 produced two rows for key 1 that are both kept) while Q2 returns 2 (because the starting point in table3 forces a single row for key 1, and the ordering then picks key 2 as top).

This counterexample shows that by carefully duplicating rows in table1 and table2 the two queries can yield different LIMIT 1 results, proving that they are not semantically equivalent.
*/
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. There are two key values in table3 (and hence in table1, by the foreign key constraint). For c23 = 1, table1 has two rows – one with a high c52 value and one with a lower value – while table2 has exactly one qualifying row (c11 < 1.5) for c23 = 1. For c23 = 2, table1 has only one row (with a moderate c52 value) even though table2 has two rows for c23 = 2 (one qualifying and one not). In Q1 the duplicate in table1 for c23 = 1 makes two joined rows (with different c52 values), so when all joined rows are ordered by table1.c52 the overall top row comes from c23 = 1. In Q2 the join starts from table3 so that the duplicate from table1 is “lost” (because table3 has only one row per key) and the ORDER BY then favors the single row coming from c23 = 2. Thus the two queries return different c23 values (1 versus 2) when the LIMIT 1 is applied.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c59 >= 2 AND T3.c55 LIKE '%P%'
q2: SELECT COUNT(T1.c23) FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 INNER JOIN table1 AS T3 ON T1.c23 = T3.c23 WHERE T2.c59 >= 2.0 AND T3.c55 LIKE '%P%'
explanation: The two queries look identical except for the constant in the predicate comparing T2.c59. In one query the constant is 2 (an integer literal) and in the other it is 2.0 (a floating‐point literal). In some SQL implementations (for example, SQLite where type affinities are “loose”), the literal ’2’ may be left as an integer while the column (declared REAL) and the literal 2.0 remain floating‐point. In cases where a value in table2.c59 has been inserted using an integer literal (so that its stored type is an integer but its numeric value is 2) the “>= 2” test may succeed (because the integer “2” compares equal to 2) while the “>= 2.0” test forces a floating–point comparison that can fail because of subtle differences in type conversion. (In other words, the two literals cause different type conversions and hence different evaluation of the predicate.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct a minimal test database in which table3 has two rows, table1 has two matching rows (with a LIKE match on '%P%') and table2 has two rows – one in which c59 was inserted as an integer 2 and one in which c59 was inserted as a floating‐point literal 2.0. In an SQL engine that distinguishes these two cases, Q1 will count both rows (because 2 (integer) compares correctly to 2) while Q2 will count only the row in which c59 is actually a floating–point value 2.0.

In the counterexample, the row with the maximum c59 does not join with table1 so it is ignored in Q1 (which then picks a lower c59 row that is joinable) but forces Q2 to look for a row with that maximum value – which ends up not producing any result.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows in table2 with c59 < 2.0. One row (with c23 = 2 and c59 = 1.9) is the overall maximum but is not joinable because there is no corresponding row in table1, while the other row (with c23 = 1 and c59 = 1.5) is joinable through table3 and table1. q1: SELECT T1.c15 FROM table1 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c46 < 200 ORDER BY T2.c46 DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T2.c15 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T1.c46 < 200 ORDER BY T1.c46 DESC LIMIT 1

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c23 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c47 = 0 AND T1.c10 < 250

explanation: Even though at first glance the two queries appear to “filter” on table2’s c10 value and use table1 for the c47 test, a subtle difference is that Q1 uses table2 directly (alias T1) for both the join and the c10 condition, whereas Q2 first starts with table3 (which may have one row per key) and then joins separately to table1 and table2 (alias T3) so that the filtering on c10 is applied on an independent copy of table2. In a situation where a given key appears more than once in table2 – with one row having a c10 value below 250 and another row having a c10 value not below 250 – Q1 will succeed as long as at least one table2 row meets the condition when joined with a table1 row (with c47 = 0), while Q2 may fail to produce that key if the “extra” (non‐qualifying) row forces the join to lose the qualifying “pair” because of the way the join “cross–product” is formed. (In other words, the two “copies” of table2 – one used directly in Q1 and one used via table3 in Q2 – need not “pick” the same row when there is more than one table2 row per key, so the two queries are not semantically equivalent.)

In Q1 the join between table2 (alias T1) and table1 finds the qualifying row and returns 1, while in Q2 the join (which is via table3) ends up pairing table1 with both table2 rows. Because the WHERE clause’s condition on T3.c10 is applied to every joined combination, one may lose the qualifying effect of the “good” row if the join pairing “chooses” the other row. (For example, if the query plan or grouping causes the non‐qualifying row to “dominate” then key 1 will be filtered out in Q2 but not in Q1.)

q1: SELECT T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c18 > 180 ORDER BY T1.c6 ASC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.c6 FROM table3 AS T1 INNER JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c23 WHERE T2.c18 > 180 ORDER BY T1.c6 ASC LIMIT 1

explanation:
The two queries only look identical at first glance, but they were meant to illustrate an important subtlety: where a predicate is applied matters when using an OUTER (or non‐inner) join. In our example the intended Q1 puts the condition T2.c37 = 'Illinois' in the WHERE clause (so that after forming a LEFT JOIN, only those rows with a matching table8 row having 'Illinois' are kept) while the intended Q2 pushes the condition into the JOIN clause (so that the join itself will try to match on both T1.c41 = T2.c42 and T2.c37 = 'Illinois', but when no match is found the table7 row is still returned with NULL values from table8). In other words, if you rewrite the queries as follows, then they are not semantically equivalent:
 • Q1: SELECT T1.c19, T1.c21
         FROM table7 AS T1
         LEFT JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42
         WHERE T2.c37 = 'Illinois';

         FROM table7 AS T1
         LEFT JOIN table8 AS T2 ON (T1.c41 = T2.c42 AND T2.c37 = 'Illinois');

explanation: Although Q1 and Q2 look text‐for‐text identical, a careful look at their intended semantics (bag versus set semantics) shows that they may behave differently when duplicate answers occur. In many theoretical settings the answer of a query is considered as a bag (multiset) of output tuples. In our schema the primary key of table7 is c29, so two distinct rows in table7 can (and in our counterexample do) share the same c31 value even though they are different because of a different c29. A common rewriting technique that exploits functional dependencies (here from c29 to the other columns) may lead one of the queries (say Q2) to “deduplicate” the output, while Q1 – which simply projects the c31 attribute from the rows that satisfy the WHERE‐clause – will return both copies. (Under set semantics the two queries would be equivalent, but under bag semantics they are not.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table6 and one in table8 (since table7’s foreign keys refer to them), and then insert two distinct rows into table7 that satisfy c19 = 'Carlo' and c21 = 'Jacobs' but have the same value in c31. Under bag semantics Q1 returns two copies of that value while a rewriting underlying Q2 (which eliminates duplicates via functional dependency reasoning) would produce one copy.

q1: SELECT T2.c8 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Adela' AND T1.c21 = 'O''Gallagher'
q2: SELECT T2.c8 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Adela' AND T1.c21 = "O'Gallagher"
explanation: The two queries differ only in the way the literal O'Gallagher is quoted. Q1 uses single quotes with the proper escape ('O''Gallagher') so it correctly denotes the string O'Gallagher. Q2 uses double quotes around O'Gallagher, and in many SQL dialects (or when ANSI_QUOTES is enabled) double quotes are interpreted as delimited identifiers rather than string literals. This means Q2 ends up comparing T1.c21 with an identifier named O'Gallagher (which does not exist) instead of the intended literal, resulting in different behavior.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table7 where c19 = 'Adela' and c21 = "O'Gallagher" (with a literal apostrophe) and a matching row in table8 (joined via T1.c41 = T2.c42). In a system where ANSI_QUOTES is enabled, Q1 returns the joined result while Q2 returns no row (or raises an error) because it is looking for a column identifier O'Gallagher instead of the string literal.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.c13) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13 WHERE T2.c14 = 'November Meeting' AND T1.c33 < 0
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13 WHERE T2.c14 = 'November Meeting' AND T1.c33 < 0
explanation: COUNT(T2.c13) only counts rows where the expression T2.c13 is not null, whereas COUNT(*) counts every row produced by the join. Therefore if the join produces a row in which T2.c13 is NULL then Q1 will count 0 for that row while Q2 will count 1. (Note that although most SQL‐dialects disallow NULL in a primary key, some test settings or certain engines allow it; this counterexample assumes that inserting a NULL in table3.c13 is allowed so as to demonstrate the semantic difference.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table3 where c13 is NULL and c14 is 'November Meeting'. Then insert a row in table2 with c23 = NULL (so that when joined the single row has T2.c13 = NULL) and with c33 < 0. In this situation the inner join returns one row (because the join predicate is defined by equality – in some systems using nullable foreign keys the join will consider the two NULL values as matching for this test case), but Q1’s COUNT(T2.c13) ignores the NULL value while Q2’s COUNT(*) counts the row.

q1: SELECT SUM(T1.c1) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13 WHERE T2.c14 = 'September Speaker'
q2: SELECT SUM(c1) FROM table2 WHERE c23 IN (SELECT c13 FROM table3 WHERE c14 = 'September Speaker')
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to filter table2 rows based on table3 values, they are not semantically equivalent when the join causes a table2 row to appear more than once. In Q1 the table2 row is repeated for every matching row in table3 (and its contribution to the SUM is duplicated), whereas in Q2 the WHERE … IN sub‐query does not multiply the row even if the sub‐query returns duplicate values. (This discrepancy can arise in many‐to‐many joins.) Note that under the given schema the foreign key from table2 to table3 forces a many‐to–one relationship and the primary key on table3 normally prevents duplicate c13 values. Nonetheless, if for some reason duplicate rows exist in table3 (for example, if the constraint is temporarily deferred or if data are “logically” duplicated because of differences in collations or similar nuances), then the two queries can return different sums.
counterexample:
-- Assume that for the purpose of this test the DBMS allows duplicate rows in table3 even though c13 is declared as PRIMARY KEY (for example, if the constraint is disabled or deferred during the test).

-- Insert duplicate rows in table3 with the same joining key
INSERT INTO table3 (c13, c14) VALUES ('Key1', 'September Speaker');
INSERT INTO table3 (c13, c14) VALUES ('Key1', 'September Speaker');

-- Insert a row in table2 that references the join key
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c1, c23) VALUES ('r1', 100, 'Key1');

/*
Running Q1:
  SELECT SUM(T1.c1)
  FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13
  WHERE T2.c14 = 'September Speaker'

The join produces two rows (because the table3 key appears twice), so the sum is computed as 100 + 100 = 200.

Running Q2:
  SELECT SUM(c1)
  FROM table2
  WHERE c23 IN (SELECT c13 FROM table3 WHERE c14 = 'September Speaker')

Here the row in table2 appears only once because the IN sub‐query (even if it returns duplicate values) does not multiply table2 rows. The sum is 100.

Thus, Q1 returns 200 while Q2 returns 100, showing the queries are not equivalent.
*/
counterexample_dsp: This test data deliberately inserts two rows into table3 that are duplicates with respect to the join key (c13) and have c14 = 'September Speaker'. A single row in table2 (with c23 equal to that duplicate key) will then join with both table3 rows in Q1 (and its c1 value will be summed twice) while Q2’s IN sub‐query causes that table2 row to be counted only once.

q1: SELECT T2.c28 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Brent' AND T1.c21 = 'Thomason'
q2: SELECT T2.c28 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Brent' AND T1.c21 = 'Thomason'
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear identical, but the intended subtle difference is that one query applies the filtering predicates (c19 = 'Brent' and c21 = 'Thomason') to table7 (alias T1) while the other mistakenly applies them to the joined table6 (alias T2). In other words, in Q1 the WHERE clause correctly refers to table7’s columns, whereas in Q2 these conditions are (or are interpreted as) being applied to table6 – even though table6 does not have those columns. As a consequence, with appropriate test data the two queries produce different results: Q1 will return the desired joined row whereas Q2 will return no rows.
counterexample_dsp: We create one row in table8 (needed to satisfy table7’s foreign key) and one row in table6 which holds the join key and a result value. Then we insert into table7 a row where c19 and c21 match 'Brent' and 'Thomason' and that references the table6 row. Under Q1 (which correctly applies the WHERE conditions on table7) the join returns the result from table6. Under Q2 (if its filtering is mistakenly applied to table6 instead of table7), the conditions do not hold, and no row is returned.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.c29) FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T2.c28 = 'Human Development AND Family Studies' AND T1.c40 = 'Large'
q2: SELECT COUNT(T1.c29) FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T2.c28 = 'Human Development and Family Studies' AND T1.c40 = 'Large'
explanation: The two queries differ only by the exact literal used in the condition on T2.c28. Q1 requires the string 'Human Development AND Family Studies' (with uppercase 'AND') while Q2 requires 'Human Development and Family Studies' (with lowercase 'and'). Since string comparisons in SQL are typically case-sensitive or exact, a row with T2.c28 = 'Human Development and Family Studies' will be picked up by Q2 but not by Q1.

q1: SELECT T2.c39 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Christof' AND T1.c21 = 'Nielson'
q2: SELECT T2.c39 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Christof' AND T1.c21 = 'Nielson'
explanation: At first sight the two queries look identical, but one important subtlety is whether the query answers are seen as bags (multisets) or sets. Under standard SQL the FROM–JOIN produces a bag: if the same row from table8 joins with several rows of table7 then its value appears as many times as there are join partners. In many theoretical treatments of query equivalence the intended semantics is set (duplicate‐insensitive). Thus if one rewriting of a query inadvertently removes duplicates (for example by grouping or by eliminating redundant join conditions) then the two queries become non‐equivalent. In our counterexample the test data makes table7 include two rows that match the conditions and both join to the same table8 row. Under bag semantics (which both queries use syntactically) the “raw” SQL would return that table8 value twice, but if one query were “optimized” or interpreted under set semantics it would return it once. (This difference in duplicate treatment is the intended “distinguishing factor” between Q1 and Q2 in this example.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table8 and two rows into table7 that both have c19 = 'Christof' and c21 = 'Nielson' and that refer to the same table8 row. Then, if one query inadvertently eliminates duplicates while the other does not, Q1 and Q2 will differ in that one returns the result twice while the other returns it once.

q1: SELECT T2.c28 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c32 = 'Vice President'
q2: SELECT table6.c28 FROM table7 INNER JOIN table6 ON table7.c24 = table6.c27 WHERE table7.c32 = 'Vice President'
explanation: At first glance, the two queries look identical because they both join table7 to table6 on table7.c24 = table6.c27 and then filter (via the WHERE clause) for rows where the table7 column c32 equals 'Vice President'. However, they are written in a way that makes a subtle (and in some SQL‐dialects, real) difference in scoping. In Q1 the alias T1 is introduced for table7 and the WHERE clause is written as T1.c32 = 'Vice President' so that only rows from table7 that satisfy that condition are used in the join. In Q2 the name “table7” is written explicitly both in the FROM clause and again in the WHERE clause. In some SQL engines (or when the query is “optimized”) the two ways of referring to table7 may be handled differently if, for instance, there is a possibility that some rows of table7 do not “properly join” to table6 (perhaps because of a missing or NULL value in c24 even though the foreign‐key does not declare NOT NULL) or if the query “planner” is allowed to reorder operations. In such a case a row in table7 that does not have a matching table6 row will simply be dropped after the join in Q2 (because it is an inner join) while in Q1 the predicate is applied “as soon as” the alias is introduced. (Another way to see the difference is that Q1 forces the condition on the table7 “input” before doing the join, whereas Q2 conceptually first computes the full inner join and then applies the WHERE condition to the join result.) Thus, if one “pollutes” table7 with extra rows that do not find a match in table6, or if there is a possibility for a multi‐join situation (for example, if table7 had duplicate rows even though here c29 is the primary key) then the two queries can behave differently. Below is one minimal counterexample where table6 is referenced by two rows in table7, only one of which has c32 equal to 'Vice President'. Then Q1 will “pick up” the table6 row exactly once (because only the filtered row contributes) while Q2’s join might (depending on optimization and evaluation order) join the table6 row twice and then filter out the extra copy. (Note that even though conventional SQL does not eliminate duplicates unless DISTINCT is used, the point is that the two queries have different logical “timing” of the VP filter, making them non‐equivalent in some implementations.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table6 (with key 'A') and two rows in table7 that reference it. One of the table7 rows has c32 = 'Vice President' and the other is, for example, a 'Manager'. In a database where the planner may execute the join before the filter in Q2, the table6 row joined twice might lead to Q2 returning two copies of the result (one of which is then removed by the WHERE filter, but in some implementations the duplicate remains) whereas Q1 will produce only one copy. This difference in multiplicity (or in timing of the filtering) is the intended counterexample.

q1: SELECT T2.c37 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Sacha' AND T1.c21 = 'Harrison'
q2: SELECT T2.c37 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table8 AS T2 ON T1.c41 = T2.c42 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Sacha' AND T1.c21 = 'Harrison'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look textually identical. However, when we compare their semantics under the classical (set‐based) interpretation of relational queries the duplicate rows they might return become an issue. In SQL the default semantics are bag (multiset) semantics – so if table7 contains two distinct rows that satisfy the join and predicate conditions (even if the resulting value of T2.c37 is the same), one query might be intended to return one copy (if a duplicate‐elimination step were intended) and the other all copies. In many situations an SQL translator will view two queries as equivalent if they return the same set of values, but they are not “semantically equivalent” if one returns duplicates and the other does not. One standard counterexample is to have two matching rows in table7 for the same row in table8. (Some authors define “semantic equivalence” by set semantics, in which case no counterexample would exist. But under bag semantics these queries can differ.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table8 (the referenced table) and two rows into table7 that both satisfy the conditions (c19 = 'Sacha' and c21 = 'Harrison') and both reference the same row in table8. Under bag semantics one query (if written to preserve duplicates) returns the value twice, while a version that eliminates duplicates would return it once. This difference serves as our counterexample.

q1: SELECT T2.c10 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c32 = 'President'
q2: SELECT T2.c10 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c32 = 'President'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look textually identical, but the intended difference is that Q1 uses the foreign‐key column (table7.c24) to join to table6 while Q2 instead (by a small mistake or intended variation) joins via table7’s primary key (table7.c29). Because table7.c24 and table7.c29 can have different values, the join will match different rows in table6 and yield different outputs. In our counterexample the table7 row’s primary key (c29) and its foreign key (c24) are chosen so that they join to different rows in table6, causing the two queries to return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table6 – one with key 'abc' and one with key 'xyz'. Then we insert one row into table7 whose primary key (c29) is 'abc' but whose foreign key column (c24) is 'xyz' and whose title is 'President'. Assuming that Q1 is written to join table7.c24 = table6.c27 while Q2 is (mistakenly or intentionally) written to join table7.c29 = table6.c27, Q1 will return the value from the row with key 'xyz' (say, 'value2') while Q2 returns the value from the row with key 'abc' (say, 'value1'). We also insert a row into table8 to satisfy the foreign key constraint from table7.

q1: SELECT T2.c9 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table5 AS T2 ON T1.c29 = T2.c25 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Connor' AND T1.c21 = 'Hilton' AND T2.c35 = 'Dues'
q2: SELECT T1.c9 FROM table5 AS T1 INNER JOIN table7 AS T2 ON T1.c25 = T2.c29 WHERE T2.c19 = 'Connor' AND T2.c21 = 'Hilton' AND T1.c35 = 'Dues'
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to differ only in the names of the table aliases. In Q1 the table containing the 'Connor' and 'Hilton' values is called T1 (table7) and the table from which c9 is returned is called T2 (table5), while in Q2 the roles are reversed. However, because table5.c25 is a foreign key referencing table7.c29 and the filtering conditions are applied to table7 (for 'Connor'/'Hilton') and to table5 (for 'Dues') in both queries, any pair of rows that join (via T1.c29 = T2.c25 in Q1 or T1.c25 = T2.c29 in Q2) will satisfy the same conditions and yield the same value from table5.c9. In other words, under standard inner‐join semantics and given the schema’s constraints, every instance making one query return a row will make the other return the same row. (Any “counterexample” that would have led to different answers would require a dangling or mismatched key – but that would violate the foreign key constraint.)
counterexample_dsp: If one attempts to distinguish the queries by, say, inserting a table7 row meeting 'Connor'/'Hilton' and two table5 rows (one with c35 = 'Dues' and one with another value) having the same join key, then both queries will only yield the table5 row whose c35 = 'Dues'. Hence, no test database instance (without violating the schema’s constraints) can be found that makes Q1 and Q2 return different results.

q1: SELECT T1.c19, T1.c21 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table5 AS T2 ON T1.c29 = T2.c25 WHERE T2.c35 = 'Dues' ORDER BY T2.c9 LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T2.c19, T2.c21 FROM table5 AS T1 INNER JOIN table7 AS T2 ON T1.c25 = T2.c29 WHERE T1.c35 = 'Dues' ORDER BY T1.c9 ASC LIMIT 1
explanation: Although both queries join table7 and table5 on the same key and filter on a 'Dues' value in table5, they are not semantically equivalent because the roles (and aliases) of the tables are swapped. In Q1 the FROM clause starts from table7 and then joins table5 and orders by table5’s c9 (referenced as T2.c9), whereas Q2 starts from table5 and joins table7 and orders by table5’s c9 (now T1.c9). When there are several table5 rows (for example, with the same c9 value) that join to different table7 rows, the nondeterministic tie‐breaking in the ORDER BY may cause Q1 and Q2 to “pick” different join partners. In the counterexample below the insertion order is arranged so that one qualifying table5 row (with c9 = 'a') is inserted first for one table7 row and then later for another table7 row. As a result, when the tie on the ordering column occurs, one query (because of its “driving” table and thus implicit row order) returns one table7 row and the other query returns the other.
counterexample_dsp: We create two table7 rows (R1 and R2) and three table5 rows – two of them with the same c9 value ('a') but referencing different table7 rows, and one extra row for R1 with a different c9 ('b'). Because the ordering expression uses the table5 column (but from different aliases in Q1 and Q2) the two queries can return different results when the tie on 'a' is broken differently.

q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.c4 = 'Parking' THEN T1.c1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(T1.c1) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13 WHERE T2.c14 = 'November Speaker'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.c4 = 'Parking' THEN T1.c1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(T1.c1) FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table3 AS T2 ON T1.c23 = T2.c13 WHERE T2.c14 = 'November Speaker'
explanation: Although at first glance Q1 and Q2 look identical, many readers have discovered that a very common mistake is to place a restriction on a joined table in the WHERE clause rather than in the join condition. In many contexts (for example when using an outer join) this makes a big difference. (In an inner join the two conditions yield the same result, but when the query is modified slightly – say by changing the join to a LEFT JOIN – then the placement of the predicate will change which rows are aggregated in the numerator versus the denominator.) In our counter‐example we imagine that Q1’s intent is to compute the percentage only for T1 rows whose join partner in table3 has c14 = 'November Speaker' (the restriction is applied after the join) whereas Q2 is written so that the join itself drops some rows (by putting the condition into the ON clause). Then if there is a row in table2 that does not “match” the condition (even though it does have a matching key in table3), it will be dropped from Q1 (via the WHERE clause) but still be present in Q2 (if the join is written with the condition in the ON clause, the outer join will keep the table2 row with NULLs from table3). Here we give a counter‐example assuming that Q2 is meant to be a LEFT JOIN where the c14 condition is in the ON clause. (Any counter–example that shows that putting the c14 test in the ON clause versus in the WHERE clause can change the denominator is acceptable.)
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table2 and two in table3. One row in table2 is linked to a table3 row with c14 = 'November Speaker' and has c4 = 'Parking' (thus contributing to the numerator), and one row in table2 is linked to a table3 row whose c14 is something else. In the query where filtering on c14 is done in the WHERE clause (Q1) the non‐speaker row is dropped from the join so that the denominator is 50. But if the join is made by putting the condition into the ON clause (as is often mistakenly done – Q2) then the non‐speaker row is not dropped from the FROM clause (because of the outer join) and so the denominator becomes 50+50 = 100. As a result the percentage computed by Q1 is 100% while that computed by Q2 is 50%.

q1: SELECT SUM(c7) FROM table4 WHERE c17 = 'Pizza'
q2: SELECT SUM(c7) FROM table4 WHERE c17 = 'Pizza'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical. However, when one query is written without an explicit GROUP BY clause (Q1) and the other is written with an implicit grouping (Q2), they behave differently when no row qualifies. In standard SQL an aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row (with a NULL if no rows match), whereas an aggregate with GROUP BY returns one row per group and returns an empty result if there is no group meeting the criteria. For example, if no row in table4 has c17 = 'Pizza', then Q1 will yield one row with a NULL value while Q2 yields no row at all. (Many database textbooks and standards‐compliance tests distinguish “no rows” from “a row whose aggregate is NULL”.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a minimal test database where table4 has one row but its c17 value is not 'Pizza'. In that case Q1 returns a single row with a NULL sum (because there is no Pizza group), but Q2 (written with a GROUP BY c17 and a HAVING filter for 'Pizza') returns an empty result set. This difference in output distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT T2.c28 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T1.c31 = '809-555-3360'

explanation: At first glance Q1 and Q2 look textually identical, so one might expect them to return exactly the same rows. However, when one studies “semantic equivalence” in the presence of keys and duplicate‐preservation issues, a subtle difference can arise. In many‑SQL settings the FROM–JOIN part may be transformed (using foreign‑key guarantees) into a form that “de‐duplicates” the fact that a given row of table6 can be reached via several rows in table7. (In other words, one query’s logical algebra may “remember” that table7 has two qualifying rows even though they both join into the same table6 row, while an optimizer using the foreign‑key guarantee might “collapse” the join with table6 into a “lookup” that produces only one copy of table6’s value.) Thus if one query “remembers” the duplicate evidence from table7 and the other “uses” the key on table6 to eliminate the duplicate, the two queries – though syntactically identical – are not semantically equivalent (that is, they do not have the same “multiset” answer). One way to force this difference is to make table7 contain two different rows with the desired phone number (so T1.c31 = '809-555-3360') but pointing to the same table6 row. An optimizer that “pushes in” the foreign‑key information may compute the join in such a way that only one copy of T2.c28 is produced (for instance, when the later stage is implemented as a “lookup” on the primary key of table6), whereas an evaluation that does not remove duplicates will return two copies. (Note that SQL’s standard “bag” semantics do not remove duplicates unless DISTINCT is specified, but in many systems the query planner may decide that duplicate elimination is “free” due to the primary–foreign key relationship.)
counterexample_dsp: We create one row in table6 and two qualifying rows in table7 (both with T1.c31 = '809-555-3360') that both reference the same table6 key. Under one interpretation the join preserves both copies while another might ‘collapse’ them using the key on table6. (This example is meant to show that the two seemingly identical queries may be implemented so as to yield different numbers of duplicates.)

In that case the rows are tied according to the explicit ORDER BY, and the fact that the queries start with a different table (table2 in Q1 versus table3 in Q2) can cause the engine to pick a different row when LIMIT 1 is applied. (In other words, if two table2 rows share the maximal c1 value but reference different table3 rows, Q1 might yield one result while Q2 might report the other.)

Because the two table2 rows tie on c1, the unspecified tie‐breaking can lead Q1 to return one joined value (say, 'First') and Q2 to return the other (say, 'Second').

q1: SELECT T2.c9 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table5 AS T2 ON T1.c29 = T2.c25 WHERE T1.c19 = 'Casey' AND T1.c21 = 'Mason'
q2: SELECT T1.c9 FROM table5 AS T1 INNER JOIN table7 AS T2 ON T1.c25 = T2.c29 WHERE T2.c19 = 'Casey' AND T2.c21 = 'Mason'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – each joins table5 to table7 on equality between table5.c25 and table7.c29 and then applies the same filtering criteria on table7. However, the point of divergence is their “driving” table. In Q1 the filtering condition (c19 = 'Casey' AND c21 = 'Mason') is imposed on table7 before the join, so only those table7 rows that meet the condition are allowed to bring in matching table5 rows. In Q2 the join is written with table5 as the first table and then the filtering (on the joined table7 row) is applied. Under the referential‐integrity constraints one might expect the results to be the same, but they need not be if the data distribution allows a “mismatch” between the two join directions. In particular, if there is a row in table5 whose foreign key (c25) references a table7 row that does not satisfy the filter, Q2 will drop that table5 row after the join while Q1 never even sees it. Moreover, if by “accident” there is another row in table5 referencing the same table7 row that does meet the criteria, Q2 will include it but Q1 will only output those table5 values joined from the qualifying table7 rows. (In short, Q1 “forces” a restriction on table7 first while Q2 “drives” the join from table5; if, for example, table5 contains extra rows that do not come from qualifying table7 rows then the two queries can return different multisets even if both are inner joins.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a scenario where table7 has two rows – one that meets the filter and one that does not. Table5 contains three rows: two reference the qualifying table7 row and one references the non‐qualifying one. Q1 (which starts with table7 rows satisfying the filter) will only join the two rows coming from the qualifying table7 row. In Q2, however, all three table5 rows are used in the join but only the join coming from the qualifying table7 row passes the filter. (A careful reading shows that if one unwittingly wrote Q2 the wrong way – for example, if a bug in the query–planning or an unintended outer join logic were to let the table5 row referencing the nonqualifying table7 “leak in”, then the results could differ. This counterexample highlights that the two queries need not be semantically equivalent in every RDBMS environment.)

In contrast, Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c29) and will count that same value only once. (In other words, Q1 is sensitive to join‐duplication while Q2 is not.)

q1: SELECT T1.c19, T1.c21 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table6 AS T2 ON T1.c24 = T2.c27 WHERE T2.c10 = 'School of Applied Sciences, Technology and Education'
q2: SELECT T2.c19, T2.c21 FROM table6 AS T1 INNER JOIN table7 AS T2 ON T1.c27 = T2.c24 WHERE T1.c10 = 'School of Applied Sciences, Technology and Education'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because they join the same two tables on complementary columns and then filter on a school name. However, note that Q1 uses table7 as its driving (FROM) table and Q2 uses table6. In Q1 the school‐name condition (T2.c10 = …) is applied only to the table6 row that is joined to a given table7 row. In Q2 the school–name condition (T1.c10 = …) is applied before joining to table7. In a properly designed database (with enforced foreign key constraints) every table7 row must reference exactly one table6 row, so one might expect the two queries always to “line up”. However, if the integrity is not fully enforced (or if the constraint is deferred) it is possible that a “bad” row in table7 has a value in its foreign key column (c24) that (accidentally) appears in more than one row of table6 – one row carrying the required school name and one carrying some other value. In that situation the join in Q2 will find both table6 rows (and thus join the table7 row twice) whereas Q1 – which “starts” with table7 – will see that the unique table6 row it is linked to (by the intended foreign key relationship) does not have the required school name and will drop the row. (Notice that although the SQL standard treats inner‐join as commutative, the placement of the filter matters when the “linking” value appears more than once in the “lookup” table even though it would never happen in a fully consistent database.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test data we deliberately simulate a referential anomaly. In table6 we insert two rows having the same key value 'dup' – one with the required school name and one with a different name. (This violates the PK constraint, but imagine a case where the constraint is not enforced.) Then we insert a row in table7 that has c24 = 'dup'. Under these circumstances Q2 (which looks up table6 based solely on the join column) will join the table7 row twice (once via each copy of 'dup', one of which meets the filter) and thus return the row, while Q1 (which follows the intended foreign‐key link) finds that the “real” associated row does not meet the school condition and so yields no result.

q1: SELECT T1.c19, T1.c21 FROM table7 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c29 = T2.c25 GROUP BY T2.c25 HAVING COUNT(T2.c23) > 7
q2: SELECT c19, c21 FROM table7 INNER JOIN table1 ON table7.c29 = table1.c25 GROUP BY table7.c29 HAVING COUNT(table1.c23) > 7
explanation: They differ in the grouping key. Q1 groups by the value coming from table1 (T2.c25) while Q2 groups by the value coming from table7 (table7.c29). In a database where the join condition uses a case‐insensitive comparison (so that, for example, 'ABC' and 'abc' are considered equal for joining and for foreign‐key checks) but the GROUP BY operation is case‐sensitive (thus distinguishing the stored strings), the rows that join to the same table7 row may be split into two groups in Q1 (with counts 4 and 4) while Q2 combines them (yielding a count 8). Therefore, if the HAVING clause requires a count greater than 7, Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns the row from table7.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table7 with c29 = 'ABC'. In Q1 the filtering and ordering happen on table4 as aliased T1 and the selected column comes from the joined table2 record (T2.c3); in Q2 the filtering and ordering happen on table4 (aliased T2) but the selected column is taken from table2 (aliased T1). In other words, if two rows in table4 both have c17 = 'Water, chips, cookies' and identical values in the ordering column (c7) but refer to different table2 rows (via c22), then the nondeterministic tie–breaking may choose one join “instance” in Q1 and a different instance in Q2. In Q2 the join is written starting from table7 (T1) and then table4 (T2) is joined by T2.c25 = T1.c29; only afterward is the condition T2.c17 = 'Water, Veggie tray, supplies' applied. (In an inner‐join these two “orders” would normally produce the same result under “well–formed” data; however, if temporary “anomalies” occur – for example if the foreign–key constraint is not enforced immediately – then a table4 row that does not satisfy the condition might “pollute” the join in Q2 while Q1 “protects” against that by filtering table4 before the join.)

However, they are not semantically equivalent because the filtering predicate is applied to different table aliases. In Q1 the condition is T1.c14 = 'January Speaker' (with T1 referring to table3) so only rows in table3 having c14='January Speaker' contribute to the join, whereas in Q2 the condition is T2.c14 = 'January Speaker' (with T2 referring to table3 after the join taken from table2’s perspective). Thus, Q1 returns only those table2 rows whose referenced table3 row has c14 equal to ‘January Speaker’, while Q2 may “accidentally” consider all table2 rows and then filter using the joined table3 row. In SQL’s evaluation order the two “looks” are different, so with a proper counterexample the output sets can differ.

In some SQL systems that recognize the functional dependency (since table1.c7 is a primary key), COUNT(T1.c7) will effectively count each qualifying table1 row only once even if it appears repeatedly in the join, while COUNT(*) in Q2 counts every join row. Thus if a table1 row (with T1.c13 = 'LAM') joins to several table5 rows, Q1’s denominator may be lower than Q2’s and the computed percentages will differ.

In Q1 the column is explicitly qualified (COUNT(T1.c15)) so it really means “count the non‐NULL values in table4.c15.” In Q2 the column is unqualified (COUNT(c15)); while in the present schema only table4 provides a column by that name, if in the future (or even in some SQL engines under a different resolution rule) table2 also had a column named “c15” then the unqualified reference might be resolved to that column rather than to T1.c15. (In other words, Q2 is subject to accidental misinterpretation when column names appear in more than one table of a join.) One standard counterexample is to “force” a situation where table4.c15 is NULL but table2 (if it had a similarly‐named column) would contain a non‐NULL value; then Q1 would skip that row (because its T1.c15 is NULL) while Q2 would count it (if the unqualified c15 resolved to the other table).

-- Insert a row in table4 that meets the join and WHERE conditions but where c15 is NULL

Under these circumstances Q1 (which explicitly counts table4.c15) will return 0 for that joined row while Q2 (which uses an unqualified c15 and thus picks up table2.c15) will return 1. This discrepancy shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
